title: Gravity and Grace
content_html:
All the natural movements of the soul are governed by laws analogous to those of material gravity. Grace alone is the exception.

One must always expect things to happen in accordance with gravity, unless there is supernatural intervention.

Two forces rule the universe: light and gravity.

Gravity. In a general way, what we expect of others is determined by the effects of gravity in ourselves; what we receive from them is determined by the effects of gravity in them. Sometimes this coincides (by chance), often not.

Why is it that as soon as a human being shows he needs another, whether a little or greatly, that other draws away? Gravity.

Lear, a tragedy of gravity. Everything we call baseness is a phenomenon of gravity. Moreover, the very word baseness indicates this.

The object of an action and the level of energy that fuels it are distinct things.

One must do such and such a thing. But where does one find the energy? A virtuous action can degrade if there is no energy available at the same level.

The base and the superficial are at the same level. He loves violently but basely: a possible sentence. He loves deeply but basely: an impossible sentence. If it is true that the same suffering is much harder to bear for a lofty motive than for a base one (the people who stood in line, motionless, from one to eight in the morning to get an egg would have found it very hard to do so to save a human life), a base virtue is perhaps in certain respects more resistant to difficulties, temptations, and misfortunes than a lofty virtue. Napoleon's soldiers. Hence the use of cruelty to maintain or restore the morale of soldiers. One must not forget this with respect to failure. It is a particular case of the law that generally puts force on the side of baseness. Gravity is like a symbol of this. Food queues. The same action is easier if the motive is base than if it is lofty. Base motives contain more energy than lofty ones. Problem: how to transfer to lofty motives the energy devoted to base ones? One must not forget that at certain moments during my headaches, when the crisis was mounting, I had an intense desire to make another human being suffer by striking them precisely at the same spot on the forehead. Analogous desires are very frequent among people. Several times in this state I yielded at least to the temptation to say hurtful words. Obedience to gravity. The greatest sin. In this way one corrupts the function of language, which is to express the relations between things.

The attitude of supplication: I must necessarily turn toward something other than myself, since it is a matter of being delivered from myself. To attempt this deliverance by means of my own energy would be like a cow pulling on its tether and thus falling to its knees. Then one releases energy in oneself through a violence that degrades it further. Compensation in the thermodynamic sense, an infernal circle from which one can only be delivered from above. The source of moral energy in human beings is external, like that of physical energy (food, breathing). One generally finds it, and this is why one has the illusion—as with physical energy—that one's being carries within itself the principle of its own preservation. Only deprivation makes one feel the need. And, in case of deprivation, one cannot help turning toward anything edible. The only remedy for this: a chlorophyll that would allow one to feed on light. Do not judge. All faults are equal. There is only one fault: not having the capacity to feed on light. For once this capacity is abolished, all faults become possible. "My food is to do the will of Him who sent me." No other good but this capacity. To descend with a movement in which gravity plays no part... Gravity makes things fall; the wing makes them rise: what wing raised to the second power can make one descend without gravity? Creation is made of the descending movement of gravity, the ascending movement of grace, and the descending movement of grace raised to the second power. Grace is the law of the descending movement. To lower oneself is to rise with regard to moral gravity. Moral gravity makes us fall upward. Too great a misfortune places a human being beneath pity: disgust, horror, and contempt. Pity descends to a certain level, and not below. How does charity manage to descend below? Do those who have fallen so low have pity on themselves?

title: Void and Compensation
content_html:
Human mechanics. Whoever suffers tries to communicate his suffering—either by ill-treating others or by arousing their pity—in order to reduce it, and he does really reduce it in this way. The one who is at the very bottom, whom no one pities, who has no power to ill-treat anyone (if he has no child or being who loves him), his suffering remains within him and poisons him.

This is as imperative as gravity. How does one free oneself from it? How does one free oneself from what is like gravity?

Tendency to spread evil outside oneself: I still have it! Beings and things are not sacred enough for me. May I never sully anything, even if I were entirely transformed into mud. May I sully nothing, even in my thought. Even in the worst moments, I would not destroy a Greek statue or a fresco by Giotto. Why then anything else? Why, for example, a moment in the life of a human being that could be a happy moment?

It is impossible to forgive whoever has done us harm if that harm has lowered us. We must think that it has not lowered us, but has revealed our true level.

Desire to see others suffer exactly what we suffer. This is why, except in periods of social instability, the resentments of the wretched are directed against their fellows.

This is a factor of social stability. Tendency to spread suffering outside oneself. If, through excessive weakness, one can neither arouse pity nor harm others, one harms one's own inner representation of the universe. Every beautiful and good thing then feels like an insult. To do harm to others is to receive something from them. What? What has one gained (and what one will have to repay) when one has done harm? One has grown. One has expanded. One has filled a void in oneself by creating one in another. To be able to harm another with impunity—for example, to vent one's anger on an inferior who is forced to keep silent—is to spare oneself an expenditure of energy, an expenditure that the other must bear. The same is true of the illegitimate satisfaction of any desire. The energy thus saved is immediately degraded. To forgive. One cannot. When someone has done us harm, reactions are created in us. The desire for revenge is a desire for essential balance. Seek balance on another plane. One must go by oneself to that limit. There one touches the void. (God helps those who help themselves...) Headaches. At a certain moment: less pain by projecting it into the universe, but the universe is altered; more acute pain, once brought back to its place, but something in me does not suffer and remains in contact with an unaltered universe. Do the same with the passions. Bring them down, reduce them to a point, and detach from them. Treat all pains in this way. Prevent them from approaching things.

The search for balance is bad because it is imaginary. Revenge. Even if one actually kills or tortures one's enemy, it is, in a sense, imaginary. The man who lived for his city, his family, his friends, to grow rich, to improve his social position, and so on—a war comes, and he is taken away as a slave, and from then on, forever, he must exhaust himself to the extreme limit of his strength simply to exist. This is atrocious, impossible, and that is why no end so miserable presents itself to him that he would not cling to it, even if it were only to have the slave working beside him punished. He no longer has the choice of ends. Any one of them is like a branch for a drowning man. Those whose city had been destroyed and who were carried off as slaves no longer had a past or a future: with what object could they fill their thoughts? With lies and the most paltry, most pitiful cravings, perhaps readier to risk crucifixion for stealing a chicken than they previously were to risk death in battle to defend their city. Certainly so, or else those dreadful punishments would not have been necessary. Otherwise, one would have had to be able to bear the void in thought. To have the strength to contemplate misfortune when one is miserable, one needs supernatural bread. The mechanism by which a situation that is too harsh degrades is that the energy provided by lofty feelings is—generally—limited; if the situation demands that one go further than this limit, one must have recourse to base feelings (fear, covetousness, the taste for records, for outward honors), which are richer in energy. This limitation is the key to many reversals. The tragedy of those who, having set out for love of the good on a path where there is suffering, arrive after a given time at their limit and debase themselves. A stone on the path. To throw oneself at the stone as if, beyond a certain intensity of desire, it should no longer exist. Or to go away as if oneself did not exist. Desire contains something absolute, and if it fails (once the energy is exhausted), the absolute is transferred to the obstacle. State of mind of the vanquished, the oppressed. To grasp (in everything) that there is a limit and that one will not go beyond it without supernatural help (or only very slightly), and that one pays for it afterward by a terrible degradation. The energy released by the disappearance of objects that constituted motives always tends to go lower. Base feelings (envy, resentment) are degraded energy. Every form of reward constitutes a degradation of energy. Self-satisfaction after a good action (or a work of art) is a degradation of higher energy. That is why the right hand must not know... A purely imaginary reward (a smile from Louis XIV) is the exact equivalent of what one has spent, because it has exactly the value of what one has spent—unlike real rewards which, as such, are above or below. Thus imaginary advantages alone provide the energy for unlimited efforts. But Louis XIV must really smile; if he does not smile, the deprivation is unspeakable. A king can only pay rewards that are mostly imaginary, or he would be insolvent. Equivalent in religion at a certain level. For want of receiving Louis XIV's smile, one fabricates a God who smiles upon us. Or else one praises oneself. One needs an equivalent reward. Inevitable, like gravity. A beloved being who disappoints. I wrote to him. It is impossible that he should not answer me what I have said to myself in his name. Others owe us what we imagine they will give us. We must forgive them this debt. To accept that they are other than the creatures of our imagination is to imitate the renunciation of God. I too am other than what I imagine myself to be. To know this is forgiveness.

title: To Accept the Void
content_html: "We hold as a tradition concerning the gods, and we see by experience concerning men, that always, by a necessity of nature, every being exercises all the power at its disposal" (Thucydides). Like a gas, the soul tends to fill the entire space granted to it. A gas that would contract and leave a void would be contrary to the law of entropy. This is not so with the God of the Christians. He is a supernatural God, whereas Jehovah is a natural God. Not to exercise all the power at one's disposal is to bear the void. This is contrary to all the laws of nature: grace alone can do it. Grace fills, but it can only enter where there is a void to receive it, and it is grace itself that makes this void. The necessity of a reward, of receiving the equivalent of what one gives. But if, doing violence to this necessity, one leaves a void, something like a suction is produced, and a supernatural reward comes. It does not come if one receives another wage: this void draws it in. The same is true of the remission of debts (this concerns not only the evil others have done us but the good we have done them). There too one accepts a void in oneself. To accept a void in oneself is supernatural. Where can one find the energy for an act that has no counterpart? The energy must come from elsewhere. Yet first there must be a tearing away, something desperate; first a void must be produced. Void: dark night. Admiration, pity (the mixture of both especially) bring real energy. But one must do without them. One must be for a time without reward, natural or supernatural. A representation of the world is needed in which there is void, so that the world may need God. This presupposes evil. To love truth means to bear the void, and consequently to accept death. Truth is on the side of death. Man escapes the laws of this world only for the duration of a flash. Instants of pause, of contemplation, of pure intuition, of mental void, of acceptance of moral void. It is through these instants that he is capable of the supernatural. Whoever bears the void for a moment either receives the supernatural bread or falls. A terrible risk, but one must run it, and even for a moment without hope. But one must not throw oneself into it.

title: Detachment
content_html:
To attain total detachment, misfortune is not enough. One needs a misfortune without consolation. One must have no consolation. No representable consolation. Then ineffable consolation descends.

To forgive debts. To accept the past without demanding compensation from the future. To halt time at the present moment. This is also the acceptance of death.

"He emptied himself of his divinity." To empty oneself of the world. To put on the nature of a slave. To reduce oneself to the point one occupies in space and time. To nothing.

To strip oneself of the imaginary royalty of the world. Absolute solitude. Then one possesses the truth of the world.

Two ways of renouncing material goods:

To deprive oneself of them in view of a spiritual good.

To conceive of and feel them as conditions of spiritual goods (for example: hunger, fatigue, humiliation cloud the intelligence and hinder meditation) and nevertheless to renounce them.

Only this second kind of renunciation is nakedness of spirit.

Moreover, material goods would scarcely be dangerous if they appeared alone and not linked to spiritual goods.

To renounce all that is not grace and not to desire grace. The extinction of desire (Buddhism)—or detachment—or amor fati—or the desire for the absolute good—are always the same thing: to empty desire, finality of all content, to desire in the void, to desire without wishing. To detach our desire from all goods and to wait. Experience proves that this waiting is fulfilled. One then touches the absolute good. In everything, beyond the particular object whatever it may be, to will in the void, to will the void. For it is a void for us, this good that we can neither represent to ourselves nor define. But this void is fuller than all fullness. If one reaches that point, one is saved, for God fills the void. This is in no way an intellectual process, in the sense we understand it today. The intelligence has nothing to find; it has only to clear the way. It is fit only for servile tasks. The good is for us a nothingness, since no thing is good. But this nothingness is not unreal. Everything that exists, compared to it, is unreal. To set aside beliefs that fill voids and sweeten bitterness. Belief in immortality. Belief in the usefulness of sins: etiam peccata. Belief in the providential ordering of events—in short, the "consolations" ordinarily sought in religion. To love God through the destruction of Troy and of Carthage, and without consolation. Love is not consolation, it is light.

The reality of the world is made by us from our attachment. It is the reality of the self transported by us into things. It is in no way external reality. That is perceptible only through total detachment. Should even a single thread remain, there is still attachment.

Misfortune that forces one to attach oneself to wretched objects lays bare the wretched character of attachment. Thereby the necessity of detachment becomes clearer.

Attachment is a manufacturer of illusions, and whoever wants reality must be detached.

As soon as one knows that something is real, one can no longer be attached to it.

Attachment is nothing other than an insufficiency in the sense of reality. One is attached to the possession of a thing because one believes that if one ceases to possess it, it ceases to exist. Many people do not feel with their whole soul that there is a world of difference between the annihilation of a city and their irremediable exile from that city.

Human misery would be intolerable if it were not diluted in time.

Prevent it from being diluted so that it may be intolerable.

"And when they had sated themselves with tears" (Iliad)—another way of making the worst suffering tolerable.

One must not weep so as not to be consoled.

All pain that does not detach is wasted pain. Nothing more dreadful: a cold desert, the soul shriveled up. Ovid. Slaves in Plautus. Never think of a thing or a being one loves without having before one's eyes the thought that perhaps this thing is destroyed or that this being is dead. Let this thought not dissolve the sense of reality, but make it more intense. Each time one says: "Thy will be done," picture to oneself all possible misfortunes taken together. Two ways of killing oneself: suicide or detachment. To kill by thought everything one loves: the only way to die. But only what one loves. (He who does not hate his father, his mother... But: love your enemies...) Not to desire that what one loves be immortal. Before a human being, whoever he may be, desire him neither immortal nor dead. The miser, through desire for his treasure, deprives himself of it. If one can place all one's good in a thing hidden in the earth, why not in God? But when God has become as full of meaning as the treasure for the miser, one must repeat forcefully to oneself that he does not exist. To feel that one loves him even if he does not exist. It is he who, through the working of the dark night, withdraws so as not to be loved like a treasure by a miser. Electra weeping for Orestes dead. If one loves God while thinking he does not exist, he will manifest his existence.

Many people do not feel with their whole soul that there is a world of difference between the annihilation of a city and their irremediable exile from that city.

Human misery would be intolerable if it were not diluted in time.

Prevent it from being diluted so that it may be intolerable.

"And when they had sated themselves with tears" (Iliad)—another way of making the worst suffering tolerable.

One must not weep so as not to be consoled.

All pain that does not detach is wasted pain. Nothing more dreadful: a cold desert, the soul shriveled up. Ovid. Slaves in Plautus. Never think of a thing or a being one loves without having before one's eyes the thought that perhaps this thing is destroyed or that this being is dead. Let this thought not dissolve the sense of reality, but make it more intense. Each time one says: "Thy will be done," picture to oneself all possible misfortunes taken together. Two ways of killing oneself: suicide or detachment. To kill by thought everything one loves: the only way to die. But only what one loves. (He who does not hate his father, his mother... But: love your enemies...) Not to desire that what one loves be immortal. Before a human being, whoever he may be, desire him neither immortal nor dead. The miser, through desire for his treasure, deprives himself of it. If one can place all one's good in a thing hidden in the earth, why not in God? But when God has become as full of meaning as the treasure for the miser, one must repeat forcefully to oneself that he does not exist. To feel that one loves him even if he does not exist. It is he who, through the working of the dark night, withdraws so as not to be loved like a treasure by a miser. Electra weeping for Orestes dead. If one loves God while thinking he does not exist, he will manifest his existence.

title: The Imagination That Fills the Void
content_html:
The imagination is continually at work filling up all the fissures through which grace might pass. Every void (that is not accepted) produces hatred, bitterness, sourness, rancor. The evil one wishes upon what one hates, and imagines, restores the balance. The militiamen of the "Spanish Testament" who invented victories in order to bear dying—an example of the void-filling imagination. Though one stands to gain nothing from victory, one can bear dying for a cause that will triumph, not for a cause that will be defeated. To do so for something utterly devoid of strength would be superhuman (the disciples of Christ). The thought of death calls for a counterweight, and this counterweight—grace apart—can only be a lie. The void-filling imagination is essentially a liar. It excludes the third dimension, for only real objects exist in three dimensions. It excludes multiple relations. Try to define things that, while actually occurring, remain in a sense imaginary. War. Crimes. Revenge. Extreme misfortune. The crimes in Spain were actually committed and yet resembled mere boasting. Realities that have no more dimensions than a dream.

In evil, as in dreams, there are no multiple readings. Hence the simplicity of criminals.

Crimes flat as dreams on both sides: the side of the executioner and the side of the victim. What is more dreadful than dying in a nightmare?

Compensations. Marius imagined future vengeance. Napoleon dreamed of posterity. Wilhelm II desired a cup of tea. His imagination was not strongly enough attached to power to span the years: it turned toward a cup of tea.

The adoration of the great by the people in the seventeenth century (La Bruyere). This was an effect of the void-filling imagination, an effect that has vanished since money took its place. Two base effects, but money more so.

In any situation whatsoever, if one halts the void-filling imagination, there is a void (poor in spirit).

In any situation (but in some, at the cost of what degradation!) the imagination can fill the void. This is how mediocre beings can be prisoners, slaves, prostitutes, and pass through any suffering without purification.

Continually suspend in oneself the work of the void-filling imagination.

If one accepts any void whatsoever, what stroke of fate can prevent one from loving the universe?

One is assured that, whatever happens, the universe is full.

title: Renunciation of Time
content_html:
Time is an image of eternity, but it is also a substitute for eternity.

The miser from whom his treasure has been taken. It is frozen past that is taken from him. Past and future, the only riches of man.

Future as void-filler. Sometimes the past plays this role too (I was, I did...). In other cases, misfortune makes the thought of happiness intolerable; it then deprives the unhappy one of his past (nessun maggior dolore...).

The past and the future hinder the salutary effect of misfortune by providing an unlimited field for imaginary elevations. That is why the renunciation of past and future is the first of all renunciations.

The present does not receive finality. Neither does the future, for it is only what will be present. But one does not know this. If one brings to bear on the present the point of that desire in us which corresponds to finality, it pierces through to the eternal.

This is the use of the despair that turns one away from the future.

When one is disappointed by a pleasure one was expecting and which comes, the cause of the disappointment is that one was expecting something from the future. And once it is here, it is the present. The future would have had to be here without ceasing to be the future. An absurdity of which only eternity is the cure.

Time and the cave. To leave the cave, to be detached, consists in no longer orienting oneself toward the future. A mode of purification: to pray to God, not only in secret with regard to men, but thinking that God does not exist. Piety toward the dead: to do everything for what does not exist. The pain of the death of another is that pain of the void, of imbalance. Efforts henceforth without object, thus without reward. If the imagination supplies a substitute, degradation. "Let the dead bury their dead." And one's own death—is it not the same? The object, the reward lie in the future. Deprivation of the future, void, imbalance. That is why "to philosophize is to learn to die." That is why "prayer is like a death." When pain and exhaustion reach the point of producing in the soul the sense of perpetuity, by contemplating this perpetuity with acceptance and love, one is torn away into eternity.

title: To Desire Without an Object
content_html:
Purification is the separation of good from covetousness.

To descend to the source of desires in order to tear the energy away from its object. It is there that desires are true as energy. It is the object that is false. But the tearing away within the soul when a desire is separated from its object is unspeakable.

If one descends into oneself, one finds that one possesses exactly what one desires.

If one desires a certain being (who is dead), one desires a particular, limited being; therefore necessarily a mortal, and one desires that being—that being who... that..., and so on—in short, that being who died on such a day, at such an hour. And one has him—dead.

If one desires money, one desires currency (an institution), something that can only be acquired under such and such conditions; so one desires it only insofar as... And to that extent, one has it.

Suffering and the void are in such cases the mode of existence of the objects of desire. Let the veil of unreality be pulled aside and one will see that they are given to us in this way.

When one sees this, one still suffers, but one is happy.

To come to know exactly what the miser has lost when his treasure was stolen: one would learn a great deal.

Lauzun and the post of captain of musketeers. He preferred being a prisoner and captain of musketeers to being free and not captain. These are garments. "They were ashamed of being naked." To lose someone: one suffers because the dead one, the absent one, has become imaginary, false. But the desire one has for him is not imaginary. Descend into oneself, to where the desire that is not imaginary resides. Hunger: one imagines foods, but the hunger itself is real: seize hold of the hunger. The presence of the dead is imaginary, but his absence is very real; it is henceforth his way of appearing. One must not seek the void, for it would be tempting God to count on supernatural bread to fill it. Nor must one flee from it. The void is the supreme fullness, but man does not have the right to know this. The proof is that Christ himself was completely ignorant of it, for a moment. One part of me must know it, but the other parts must not, for if they knew it in their base way, there would no longer be any void. Christ had all of human misery, except sin. But he had all that makes man capable of sin. What makes man capable of sin is the void. All sins are attempts to fill voids. Thus my life, full of stains, is close to his perfectly pure life, and so too with lives much more base. However low I fall, I shall not be far from him. But this, if I fall, I shall no longer be able to know. The handshake of a friend seen again after a long absence. I do not even notice whether for the sense of touch it is a pleasure or a pain: as the blind man directly feels objects at the end of his stick, I directly feel the presence of my friend. It is the same with the circumstances of life, whatever they may be, and God. This implies that one must never seek consolation for pain. For felicity is beyond the domain of consolation and pain. It is perceived with another sense, just as the perception of objects at the end of a stick or an instrument is other than the sense of touch properly speaking. This other sense is formed by the displacement of attention through an apprenticeship in which the whole soul and the body participate. That is why in the Gospel: "I tell you, those people have received their reward." One must have no compensation. It is the void in the sensibility that carries one beyond sensibility. The denial of Saint Peter. To say to Christ: I will remain faithful to you, was already to deny him, for it meant supposing the source of faithfulness to be in oneself and not in grace. Fortunately, since he was chosen, this denial became manifest to all and to himself. In how many others, such boasts are fulfilled—and they never understand. It was difficult to be faithful to Christ. It was a faithfulness in the void. Much easier to be faithful unto death to Napoleon. Much easier for the martyrs, later, to be faithful, for the Church already existed, a force, with temporal promises. One dies for what is strong, not for what is weak, or at least for what, being momentarily weak, retains an aura of strength. Faithfulness to Napoleon at Saint Helena was not a faithfulness in the void. To die for what is strong strips death of its bitterness. And, at the same time, of all its value. To supplicate a man is a desperate attempt to force one's own system of values into the mind of another, through sheer intensity. To supplicate God is the opposite: an attempt to make divine values pass into one's own soul. Far from thinking as intensely as one can about the values to which one is attached, it is an interior void.

title: The Self
content_html:
We possess nothing in the world—for chance can take everything from us—except the power to say I. That is what must be given to God, that is to say, destroyed. There is absolutely no other free act permitted to us, except the destruction of the I. Offering: one cannot offer anything other than the I, and everything one calls offering is nothing but a label placed on a revenge of the I. Nothing in the world can take from us the power to say I. Nothing, except extreme misfortune. Nothing is worse than extreme misfortune which from the outside destroys the I, since from then on one can no longer destroy it oneself. What happens to those in whom misfortune has destroyed the I from the outside? One can only imagine for them annihilation in the manner of the atheist or materialist conception. That they have lost the I does not mean they no longer have any selfishness. On the contrary. True, it does sometimes happen that a dog-like devotion is produced. But at other times the being is on the contrary reduced to naked, vegetative selfishness. A selfishness without an I. If one has even slightly begun the process of destroying the I, one can prevent any misfortune from doing harm. For the I is not destroyed by external pressure without extreme revolt. If one refuses this revolt out of love for God, then the destruction of the I does not take place from the outside, but from within.

Redemptive suffering. When the human being is in a state of perfection, when with the help of grace he has completely destroyed the I in himself, if he then falls to the degree of misfortune that would correspond for him to the destruction of the I from the outside, that is the fullness of the cross. Misfortune can no longer in him destroy the I, for the I in him no longer exists, having entirely disappeared and left its place to God. But misfortune produces an effect equivalent, on the plane of perfection, to the external destruction of the I. It produces the absence of God. "My God, why hast thou forsaken me?"

What is this absence of God produced by extreme misfortune in the perfect soul? What is this value attached to it that is called redemptive suffering?

Redemptive suffering is that by which evil truly has the fullness of being, to the extent that it can receive it.

Through redemptive suffering, God is present in extreme evil. For the absence of God is the mode of divine presence that corresponds to evil—the felt absence. Whoever does not have God within cannot feel his absence.

This is the purity, the perfection, the fullness, the abyss of evil. Whereas hell is a false abyss (cf. Thibon). Hell is superficial. Hell is nothingness pretending and giving the illusion of being.

The purely external destruction of the I is nearly infernal suffering. The external destruction to which the soul associates itself through love is expiatory suffering. The production of the absence of God in the soul completely emptied of itself through love is redemptive suffering. In misfortune, the survival instinct outlasts the attachments that have been torn away and blindly clings to anything that can serve as support, as a plant clings with its tendrils. Gratitude (except in a base form), justice are not conceivable in this state. Slavery. There is no longer that surplus quantity of energy that supports free will, by means of which man gains distance. Misfortune, in this aspect, is hideous, as life is always hideous when laid bare, like a stump, like the swarming of insects. Life without form. To survive is there the sole attachment. It is there that extreme misfortune begins, when all attachments are replaced by that of surviving. Attachment appears there in its nakedness. Without any other object than itself. Hell. It is through this mechanism that nothing seems sweeter to the wretched than life, even though their life is in no way preferable to death. In this situation, to accept death is total detachment. Near-hell on earth. Extreme uprooting in misfortune. Human injustice generally produces not martyrs but near-damned. Those who have fallen into near-hell are like the man stripped and wounded by robbers. They have lost the garment of character. The greatest suffering that leaves roots intact is still at an infinite distance from near-hell.

When one renders service to beings thus uprooted and receives in return bad treatment, ingratitude, betrayal, one is simply undergoing a small part of their misfortune. One has the duty to expose oneself to it, within measure, as one has the power to expose oneself to misfortune. When it happens, one must bear it as one bears misfortune, without connecting it to particular persons, for it does not connect to them. There is something impersonal in near-infernal misfortune, as in perfection. For those in whom the I is dead, nothing can be done, absolutely nothing. But one never knows whether, in a given human being, the I is entirely dead or merely unconscious. If it is not entirely dead, love can revive it as though by an injection, but only love that is entirely pure, without the slightest trace of condescension, for the slightest shade of contempt pushes toward death. When the I is wounded from the outside, its first reaction is the most extreme, the most bitter revolt, like an animal struggling. But once the I is half dead, it desires to be finished off and lets itself sink into unconsciousness. If then a touch of love awakens it, the pain is extreme and produces anger and sometimes hatred toward the one who caused that pain. Hence, in fallen beings, those apparently inexplicable reactions of vengeance against the benefactor. It also happens that in the benefactor the love is not pure. Then the I, awakened by love and immediately receiving a new wound through contempt, the most bitter hatred arises—a legitimate hatred. The one in whom the I is entirely dead, on the contrary, is in no way troubled by the love shown to him. He lets himself be handled like dogs and cats that receive food, warmth, and caresses, and like them he is eager to receive as much as possible. Depending on the case, he becomes attached like a dog or lets himself be handled with a kind of indifference like a cat. He drinks without the slightest scruple all the energy of whoever takes care of him.

Unfortunately, every charitable work risks having as its clients a majority of unscrupulous people, or above all beings in whom the I has been killed.

The I is killed more quickly the weaker the character of the one who suffers misfortune. More precisely, the limiting misfortune, the misfortune that destroys the I, is situated more or less far away depending on the temper of the character, and the farther it is situated, the more one says the character is strong.

The more or less remote location of this limit is probably a fact of nature, like aptitude for mathematics, and whoever, having no faith, is proud of having kept up "good morale" in difficult circumstances is no more right than the adolescent who takes pride in having a gift for mathematics. The one who believes in God runs the risk of an even greater illusion, namely, of attributing to grace what is simply an effect of nature, essentially mechanical.

The anguish of extreme misfortune is the external destruction of the I. Arnolphe, Phaedra, Lycaon. One is right to fall to one's knees, to supplicate basely, when the violent death about to strike is going to kill the I from the outside before even life is destroyed.

"Niobe too, she of the beautiful hair, thought of eating." This is sublime in the manner of space in the frescoes of Giotto.

A humiliation that forces one to renounce even despair.

The sin in me says I.

I am everything. But this I is God. And it is not an I.

Evil creates the distinction; it prevents God from being equivalent to everything.

It is my misery that makes me I. It is the misery of the universe that makes God, in a sense, I (that is, a person).

The Pharisees were people who relied on their own strength to be virtuous.

Humility consists in knowing that in what one calls I there is no source of energy by which one can rise.

All that is precious in me, without exception, comes from somewhere other than myself, not as a gift, but as a loan that must be ceaselessly renewed. All that is in me, without exception, is absolutely without value; and, among the gifts come from elsewhere, everything I appropriate immediately becomes without value. Perfect joy excludes even the feeling of joy, for in the soul filled by its object no corner is available to say I. One does not imagine such joys when they are absent, and thus the incentive to seek them is lacking.

One has the duty to expose oneself to it, within measure, as one has the power to expose oneself to misfortune. When it happens, one must bear it as one bears misfortune, without connecting it to particular persons, for it does not connect to them. There is something impersonal in near-infernal misfortune, as in perfection. For those in whom the I is dead, nothing can be done, absolutely nothing. But one never knows whether, in a given human being, the I is entirely dead or merely unconscious. If it is not entirely dead, love can revive it as though by an injection, but only love that is entirely pure, without the slightest trace of condescension, for the slightest shade of contempt pushes toward death. When the I is wounded from the outside, its first reaction is the most extreme, the most bitter revolt, like an animal struggling. But once the I is half dead, it desires to be finished off and lets itself sink into unconsciousness. If then a touch of love awakens it, the pain is extreme and produces anger and sometimes hatred toward the one who caused that pain. Hence, in fallen beings, those apparently inexplicable reactions of vengeance against the benefactor. It also happens that in the benefactor the love is not pure. Then the I, awakened by love and immediately receiving a new wound through contempt, the most bitter hatred arises—a legitimate hatred. The one in whom the I is entirely dead, on the contrary, is in no way troubled by the love shown to him. He lets himself be handled like dogs and cats that receive food, warmth, and caresses, and like them he is eager to receive as much as possible. Depending on the case, he becomes attached like a dog or lets himself be handled with a kind of indifference like a cat. He drinks without the slightest scruple all the energy of whoever takes care of him.

Unfortunately, every charitable work risks having as its clients a majority of unscrupulous people, or above all beings in whom the I has been killed.

The I is killed more quickly the weaker the character of the one who suffers misfortune. More precisely, the limiting misfortune, the misfortune that destroys the I, is situated more or less far away depending on the temper of the character, and the farther it is situated, the more one says the character is strong.

The more or less remote location of this limit is probably a fact of nature, like aptitude for mathematics, and whoever, having no faith, is proud of having kept up "good morale" in difficult circumstances is no more right than the adolescent who takes pride in having a gift for mathematics. The one who believes in God runs the risk of an even greater illusion, namely, of attributing to grace what is simply an effect of nature, essentially mechanical.

The anguish of extreme misfortune is the external destruction of the I. Arnolphe, Phaedra, Lycaon. One is right to fall to one's knees, to supplicate basely, when the violent death about to strike is going to kill the I from the outside before even life is destroyed.

"Niobe too, she of the beautiful hair, thought of eating." This is sublime in the manner of space in the frescoes of Giotto.

A humiliation that forces one to renounce even despair.

The sin in me says I.

I am everything. But this I is God. And it is not an I.

Evil creates the distinction; it prevents God from being equivalent to everything.

It is my misery that makes me I. It is the misery of the universe that makes God, in a sense, I (that is, a person).

The Pharisees were people who relied on their own strength to be virtuous.

Humility consists in knowing that in what one calls I there is no source of energy by which one can rise.

All that is precious in me, without exception, comes from somewhere other than myself, not as a gift, but as a loan that must be ceaselessly renewed. All that is in me, without exception, is absolutely without value; and, among the gifts come from elsewhere, everything I appropriate immediately becomes without value. Perfect joy excludes even the feeling of joy, for in the soul filled by its object no corner is available to say I. One does not imagine such joys when they are absent, and thus the incentive to seek them is lacking.
excerpt: We possess nothing in the world—for chance can take everything from us—except the power to say I. That is what must be given to God, that is to say, destroyed. There is absolutely no other free act...

title: Decreation
content_html:
Decreation: to make the created pass into the uncreated. Destruction: to make the created pass into nothingness. A guilty substitute for decreation. Creation is an act of love, and it is perpetual. At every instant our existence is the love of God for us. But God can love only himself. His love for us is love for himself through us. Thus he who gives us being loves in us the consent not to be. Our existence is made solely of his waiting, of our consent not to exist. Perpetually, he begs from us this existence that he gives us. He gives it to us in order to beg it from us. Inflexible necessity, misery, distress, the crushing weight of need and of labor that exhausts, cruelty, torture, violent death, constraint, terror, illness—all this is divine love. It is God who out of love withdraws from us so that we may love him. For if we were exposed to the direct radiation of his love, without the protection of space, time, and matter, we would be evaporated like water in the sun; there would not be enough I in us to surrender the I out of love. Necessity is the screen placed between God and us so that we may be. It is for us to pierce the screen in order to cease to be. There exists a "deifugal" force. Otherwise everything would be God.

Man has been given an imaginary divinity so that he may strip himself of it like Christ stripped himself of his real divinity.

Renunciation. Imitation of the renunciation of God in creation. God renounces—in a sense—being everything. We must renounce being something. This is the only good for us.

We are bottomless barrels as long as we have not understood that we have a bottom.

Elevation and abasement. A woman who looks at herself in a mirror and adorns herself does not feel the shame of reducing herself, this infinite being who beholds all things, to a small space. Likewise, every time one raises the self (the social, psychological self, etc.), however high one raises it, one infinitely degrades oneself by reducing oneself to being only that. When the self is abased (unless energy tends to raise it in desire), one knows that one is not that.

A very beautiful woman who looks at her image in the mirror may very well believe that she is that. An ugly woman knows she is not that.

Everything grasped by the natural faculties is hypothetical. Only supernatural love posits. Thus we are co-creators.

We participate in the creation of the world by decreating ourselves.

One possesses only what one renounces. What one does not renounce escapes us. In this sense, one cannot possess anything without passing through God.

Catholic communion. God did not only once become flesh; he becomes matter every day to give himself to man and to be consumed by him. Reciprocally, through fatigue, misfortune, death, man is made matter and consumed by God. How can one refuse this reciprocity? He emptied himself of his divinity. We must empty ourselves of the false divinity with which we were born. Once one has understood that one is nothing, the goal of all efforts is to become nothing. It is to this end that one suffers with acceptance, it is to this end that one acts, it is to this end that one prays. My God, grant me to become nothing. As I become nothing, God loves himself through me. What is below resembles what is above. Thereby slavery is an image of obedience to God, humiliation an image of humility, physical necessity an image of the irresistible thrust of grace, the abandonment of saints to the day-by-day an image of the fragmentation of time among criminals and prostitutes, and so on. On this account, one must seek what is lowest, as an image. Let what is base in us go downward so that what is high may rise upward. For we are inverted. We are born thus. To re-establish order is to undo the creature in us. Reversal of the objective and the subjective. Likewise, reversal of the positive and the negative. This is also the meaning of the philosophy of the Upanishads.

We are born and live in the wrong direction, for we are born and live in sin, which is a reversal of the hierarchy. The first operation is the reversal. Conversion. Unless the grain dies... It must die in order to release the energy it carries within itself so that new combinations may be formed. Likewise, we must die in order to release the attached energy, to possess a free energy capable of conforming to the true relation of things. The extreme difficulty I often find in carrying out the slightest action is a favor granted to me. For thus, with ordinary actions and without attracting attention, I can cut the roots of the tree. However detached one may be from opinion, extraordinary actions contain a stimulus one cannot remove from them. This stimulus is entirely absent from ordinary actions. To find extraordinary difficulty in performing an ordinary action is a favor for which one must be grateful. One must not ask for this difficulty to disappear; one must implore the grace to make use of it. In general, do not wish for the disappearance of any of one's miseries, but for the grace that transfigures them. Physical suffering (and deprivations) are often for courageous men a test of endurance and strength of soul. But there is a better use for them. Let them not be that for me. Let them be a sensible testimony to human misery. Let me undergo them in an entirely passive way. Whatever happens, how could I ever find misfortune too great, since the bite of misfortune and the degradation to which it condemns enable the knowledge of human misery, a knowledge that is the gateway to all wisdom?

But pleasure, happiness, prosperity, if one knows how to recognize in them what comes from outside (from chance, from circumstances, etc.), also bear witness to human misery. Make this use of them too. And even of grace, insofar as it is a sensible phenomenon...

To be nothing in order to be in one's true place in the whole.

Renunciation requires that one pass through anguish equivalent to that which would be caused in reality by the loss of all beloved beings and of all goods, including faculties and acquisitions in the order of intelligence and character, opinions and beliefs about what is good and what is stable, and so on. And all this one must not take from oneself, but lose—like Job. But the energy thus cut off from its object must not be squandered in oscillations, degraded. The anguish must therefore be still greater than in real misfortune; it must not be fragmented over time nor directed toward a hope.

When the passion of love reaches down to the vegetative energy, then one has cases like Phaedra, Arnolphe, and so on. "And I feel deep inside that I shall have to die of it..."

Hippolytus is truly more necessary to Phaedra's life, in the most literal sense, than food.

For the love of God to penetrate so low, nature must have undergone the ultimate violence. Job, the cross...

The love of Phaedra, of Arnolphe, is impure. A love that would descend so low and that would be pure...

To become nothing down to the vegetative level; it is then that God becomes bread. If we consider ourselves at a determinate moment—the present instant, cut off from past and future—we are innocent. We cannot at that instant be other than what we are: all progress implies duration. It is in the order of the world, at that instant, that we should be such as we are. To isolate an instant thus implies forgiveness. But this isolation is detachment. There are only two instants of perfect nakedness and purity in human life: birth and death. One cannot worship God in human form without sullying the divinity except as a newborn and as one in agony. Death. An instantaneous state, without past or future. Indispensable for the access to eternity. If one finds the fullness of joy in the thought that God is, one must find the same fullness in the knowledge that oneself one is not, for it is the same thought. And this knowledge is extended to the sensibility only through suffering and death. Joy in God. There is truly perfect and infinite joy in God. My participation can add nothing, my non-participation can take away nothing from the reality of this perfect and infinite joy. From then on, what does it matter whether I should have part in it or not? No importance at all. Those who desire their salvation do not truly believe in the reality of joy in God. The belief in immortality is harmful because it is not in our power to represent the soul as truly incorporeal. Thus this belief is in fact belief in the prolongation of life, and it removes the use of death. Presence of God. This must be understood in two ways. Insofar as he is Creator, God is present in everything that exists, from the moment it exists. The presence for which God needs the cooperation of the creature is the presence of God, not insofar as he is the Creator, but insofar as he is the Spirit. The first presence is the presence of creation. The second is the presence of decreation. (He who created us without ourselves will not save us without ourselves. Saint Augustine.) God could create only by hiding himself. Otherwise there would be nothing but him. Holiness must therefore also be hidden, even from consciousness to a certain degree. And it must be hidden in the world. Being and having. Man does not have being; he has only having. The being of man is situated behind the curtain, on the side of the supernatural. What he can know of himself is only what circumstances lend him. I is hidden from me (and from others); it is on the side of God, it is in God, it is God. To be proud is to forget that one is God... The curtain is human misery: there was a curtain even for Christ. Job. Satan to God: Does he love you gratuitously? It is a matter of the level of love. Is the love situated at the level of sheep, of wheat fields, of many children? Or further, in the third dimension, behind? However deep this love may be, there is a moment of rupture at which it succumbs, and it is the moment that transforms, that tears from the finite toward the infinite, that makes the soul's love for God transcendent in the soul. It is the death of the soul. Woe to the one for whom the death of the body precedes that of the soul! The soul that is not full of love dies a bad death. Why must such a death fall indiscriminately? It must. Everything must fall indiscriminately. Appearance clings to being, and only pain can tear them apart. Whoever has being cannot have appearance. Appearance chains being. The course of time tears seeming from being and being from seeming, by violence. Time reveals that it is not eternity. One must uproot oneself. Cut down the tree and make of it a cross, and then carry it every day. One must not be I, but still less must one be we. The city gives the sense of being at home. Acquire the sense of being at home in exile. Be rooted in the absence of a place. Uproot oneself socially and vegetatively. Exile oneself from every earthly homeland. To do all this to others, from without, is a substitute for decreation. It produces unreality. But in uprooting oneself, one seeks greater reality.

title: Self-Effacement
content_html:
God gave me being so that I might give it back to him. It is like one of those tests that resemble traps, found in fairy tales and initiation stories. If I accept this gift, it is bad and fatal; its virtue appears through refusal. God allows me to exist outside of him. It is for me to refuse this permission. Humility is the refusal to exist outside of God. Queen of virtues. The self is only the shadow projected by sin and error that arrest the light of God, and that I take for a being. Even if one could be like God, it would be better to be mud that obeys God. What a pencil is for me when, with eyes closed, I feel the table with its point—to be that for Christ. We have the possibility of being mediators between God and the part of creation entrusted to us. Our consent is needed so that through us he may perceive his own creation. With our consent he performs this marvel. It would suffice that I had known how to withdraw from my own soul for this table before me to have the incomparable good fortune of being seen by God. God can love in us only this consent to withdraw in order to let him pass, just as he himself, as Creator, withdrew in order to let us be. This double operation has no other meaning than love, like the father who gives his child something with which the child can make a present on the father's birthday. God, who is nothing other than love, has created nothing other than love. All the things I see, hear, breathe, touch, eat, all the beings I encounter—I deprive all of this of contact with God, and I deprive God of contact with all of this, to the extent that something in me says I. I can do something for all of this and for God, namely withdraw, respect the intimate encounter. The strict fulfillment of simply human duty is a condition for my being able to withdraw. It gradually wears away the ropes that hold me in place and prevent me. I cannot conceive the necessity that God should love me, when I feel so clearly that even among human beings affection for me can only be a mistake. But I can easily picture him loving this perspective of creation that can only be had from the point where I am. But I stand in the way. I must withdraw so that he may see it. I must withdraw so that God may come into contact with the beings whom chance places in my path and whom he loves. My presence is indiscreet, as though I found myself between two lovers or two friends. I am not the young girl awaiting a bridegroom, but the unwanted third who is with two betrothed and must go away so that they may truly be together. If only I knew how to disappear, there would be a perfect union of love between God and the earth I walk on, the sea I hear... What does it matter what energy, what gifts I have, and so on? I always have enough of them to disappear.

"And death, ravishing the light from my eyes, restores to the day they soiled all its purity..."

Let me disappear so that these things I see may become, by virtue of no longer being things that I see, perfectly beautiful. I do not in the least desire that this created world should no longer be perceptible to me, but that it should no longer be to me that it is perceptible. To me, it cannot tell its secret, which is too high. Let me depart, and the creator and the creature will exchange their secrets. To see a landscape as it is when I am not there... When I am somewhere, I sully the silence of heaven and earth with my breathing and the beating of my heart.

title: Necessity and Obedience
content_html:
The sun shines on the just and on the unjust. God makes himself necessity. Two faces of necessity: exercised and undergone. Sun and cross. To accept being subject to necessity and to act only by handling it. Subordination: economy of energy. Thanks to it, an act of heroism can be accomplished without either the one who commands or the one who obeys needing to be heroes. To come to receive orders from God. In which cases does the struggle against a temptation exhaust the energy attached to good, and in which cases does it raise that energy on the scale of qualities of energy? This must depend on the respective importance of the roles of will and attention. One must deserve, through love, to undergo constraint. Obedience is the supreme virtue. To love necessity. Necessity is what is lowest in relation to the individual (constraint, force, a "hard necessity"), but universal necessity delivers us from it. There are cases where a thing is necessary solely because it is possible. For example, eating when one is hungry, giving water to a wounded man dying of thirst when water is close by. Neither a bandit nor a saint would refrain from it.

By analogy, to discern the cases where, though it does not appear so clearly at first sight, possibility implies necessity. To act in those cases and not in others.

The pomegranate seed. One does not commit oneself to loving God; one consents to the commitment that has been made within oneself without oneself.

To perform only, by way of virtuous acts, those one cannot help performing, those one cannot not do, but to increase ceaselessly through well-directed attention the number of those one cannot not do.

Not to take a single step, even toward the good, beyond what one is irresistibly driven to by God, and this in action, in speech, and in thought. But to be ready under his impulse to go anywhere, to the very limit (the cross...). To be ready to the utmost is to pray to be driven, but without knowing where.

If my eternal salvation were on this table in the form of an object and I had only to reach out my hand to seize it, I would not extend my hand without having received the order to do so.

Detachment from the fruits of action. To withdraw from that fatality. How?

To act, not for an object, but by a necessity. I cannot do otherwise. It is not an action, but a kind of passivity. Non-acting action.

The slave is, in a sense, a model (the lowest... the highest... always the same law). Matter too.

To transfer outside oneself the motives of one's actions. To be driven. Motives that are entirely pure (or the vilest: always the same law) appear as external.

For every act, consider it from the aspect not of its object, but of its impulse. Not: to what end? But: where does it come from?

"I was naked and you clothed me." This gift is simply the sign of the state in which those who acted thus found themselves. They were in a state such that they could not help feeding those who were hungry, clothing those who were naked; they did not do it in any way for Christ; they could not help doing it because the compassion of Christ was in them. Just as Saint Nicholas, going with Saint Cassian across the Russian steppe to a meeting with God, could not help missing the appointed hour in order to help a peasant free his cart stuck in the mud. The good accomplished thus almost in spite of oneself, almost with shame and remorse, is pure. All absolutely pure good entirely escapes the will. Good is transcendent. God is the Good.

"I was hungry and you helped me." When, Lord? They did not know. One must not know.

One must not help one's neighbor for Christ, but through Christ. Let the self disappear in such a way that Christ, by means of the intermediary constituted by our soul and our body, helps one's neighbor. To be the slave whom his master sends to bring such help to such an unfortunate person. The help comes from the master, but it is addressed to the unfortunate person. Christ did not suffer for his Father. He suffered for mankind by the will of the Father.

One cannot say of the slave who goes to bring help that he does it for his master. He does nothing. Even if, to reach the unfortunate person, he walked on nails with bare feet, then he suffers, but he does nothing. For he is a slave. "We are unprofitable slaves," that is to say: we have done nothing. In general, for God is a bad expression. God must not be put in the dative. Not to go to one's neighbor for God, but to be driven by God toward one's neighbor as the arrow toward the target by the archer. To be only an intermediary between uncultivated land and plowed field, between the data of a problem and the solution, between the blank page and the poem, between the hungry wretch and the satisfied wretch. In all things, only what comes to us from outside, gratuitously, by surprise, as a gift of fate, without our having sought it, is pure joy. Correspondingly, true good can only come from outside, never from our effort. In no case can we manufacture something better than ourselves. Thus the effort truly directed toward the good must not succeed: it is after a long and sterile straining that ends in despair, when one expects nothing more, that from outside, a marvelous surprise, the gift comes. This effort has destroyed a part of the false fullness within us. The divine void, fuller than fullness, has come to dwell in us. The will of God. How to know it? If one makes silence within oneself, if one silences all desires, all opinions, and thinks with love, with all one's soul and without words: "Thy will be done," what one then feels without uncertainty that one must do (even though, in certain respects, it might be an error) is the will of God. For if one asks him for bread, he does not give stones.

Convergent criterion. An action or an attitude in favor of which reason finds several distinct and convergent motives, but which one feels exceeds all representable motives.

One must have no particular thing in view in prayer, unless one has received supernatural inspiration for it. For God is the universal being. Certainly he descends into the particular. He descended, he descends in the act of creation; likewise the Incarnation, the Eucharist, Inspiration, etc. But it is a descending movement, never an ascending one, a movement of God, not of us. We can only bring about such a connection insofar as God dictates it to us. Our role is to be turned toward the universal.

This is perhaps the solution to Berger's difficulty about the impossibility of connecting the relative to the absolute. It is impossible by an ascending movement, but possible by a descending movement.

One can never know that God commands a given thing. The intention oriented toward obedience to God saves, whatever one does, if one places God infinitely above oneself, and damns, whatever one does, if one calls God one's own heart. In the first case, one never thinks that what one has done, is doing, or will do could be a good.

The use of temptations. It is bound up with the relationship of the soul to time. To contemplate a possible evil for a long time without carrying it out brings about a kind of transubstantiation. If one resists with a finite energy, this energy is exhausted in a given time, and when it is exhausted, one yields. If one remains motionless and attentive, it is the temptation that exhausts itself — and one harvests the upgraded energy. If one contemplates in the same way a possible good — motionless and attentive — a transubstantiation of energy also takes place, by which one carries out this good. The transubstantiation of energy consists in this: that, for the good, there comes a moment when one cannot not accomplish it. From this also follows a criterion of good and evil. Each creature who has attained perfect obedience constitutes a singular, unique, irreplaceable mode of presence, knowledge, and operation of God in the world. Necessity. To see the relations of things, and oneself, including the ends one carries within oneself, as one of the terms. Action follows naturally from this. Obedience: there are two kinds. One can obey gravity or the relation of things. In the first case, one does what the void-filling imagination pushes one toward. One can attach to it, and often with plausibility, all labels including good and God. If one suspends the work of the void-filling imagination and fixes one's attention on the relation of things, a necessity appears that one cannot not obey. Until then, one has neither the notion of necessity nor the feeling of obedience.

Then one cannot be proud of what one accomplishes, even if one accomplished wonders. The words of the Breton cabin boy to the journalist who asked him how he could have done that: "Had to be done!" The purest heroism. It is found among the common people more than elsewhere. Obedience is the only pure motive, the only one that does not enclose to any degree the reward of the action and leaves all care of the reward to the Father who is in secret, who sees in secret. On condition that it is obedience to a necessity, not to a constraint (terrible void in slaves). Whatever one gives of oneself to others or to a great object, whatever suffering one endures, if it is through pure obedience to a clear conception of the relation of things and to necessity, one commits to it without effort, though one accomplishes it with effort. One cannot do otherwise, and there results no recoil, no void to fill, no desire for reward, no resentment, no abasement. Action is the indicating needle of the scale. One must not touch the needle, but the weights. It is exactly the same for opinions. From that point, either confusion or suffering. Foolish virgins. — This means that at the moment one becomes aware that there is a choice to be made, the choice is already made — in one direction or the other. Much truer than the allegory of Hercules between vice and virtue. When in man nature, being cut off from all carnal impulse and deprived of all supernatural light, performs actions in conformity with what supernatural light would impose were it present, that is the fullness of purity. This is the central point of the Passion. The right relationship with God is, in contemplation, love, and in action, slavery. Do not mix them. To act as a slave while contemplating with love...
