title: Illusions
content_html:
One moves toward a thing because one believes it is good, and one remains chained to it because it has become necessary. Sensible things are real as sensible things, but unreal as goods. Appearance has the fullness of reality, but as appearance. As something other than appearance, it is error. The illusion concerning the things of this world does not concern their existence, but their value. The image of the cave refers to value. We possess only shadows of imitations of good. It is also in relation to good that we are captive, chained (attachment). We accept the false values that appear to us, and when we believe we are acting, we are in reality motionless, for we remain in the same system of values. Acts effectively carried out and yet imaginary. A man attempts suicide, survives, and is no more detached afterward than before. His suicide was imaginary. Suicide is no doubt always imaginary, and that is why it is forbidden. Time, strictly speaking, does not exist (except the present as a limit), and yet it is to this that we are subject. Such is our condition. We are subject to what does not exist. Whether it is a matter of passively endured duration — physical pain, waiting, regret, remorse, fear — or of time handled — order, method, necessity — in both cases, that to which we are subject does not exist. But our subjection exists. We are really bound by unreal chains. Time, being unreal, veils all things and ourselves in unreality. The treasure, for the miser, is the shadow of an imitation of good. It is doubly unreal. For a means (money) is already, as such, something other than a good. But taken outside its function as a means, erected as an end, it is even further from being a good. It is in relation to value judgments that sensations are unreal; it is as values that things are unreal for us. But the attribution of a false value to an object also removes reality from the perception of that object, for it drowns perception in imagination. Thus perfect detachment alone allows one to see things bare, outside that fog of lying values. This is why Job needed boils and a dunghill for the beauty of the world to be revealed to him. For there is no detachment without pain. And there is no pain endured without hatred and without falsehood without there also being detachment. The soul that has passed its head beyond heaven feeds on being. The one inside feeds on opinion. Necessity is essentially foreign to the imaginary. What is real in perception and distinguishes it from dreams is not sensations; it is the necessity enveloped in those sensations. "Why these things and not others?"

"It is so." In the spiritual life, illusion and truth are distinguished in the same way. What is real in perception and distinguishes it from dreams is not sensations; it is necessity. Distinction between those who remain in the cave, close their eyes, and imagine the journey, and those who make it. Real and imaginary in the spiritual realm too, and there too necessity makes the difference. Not suffering simply, for there are imaginary sufferings. As for inner feeling, nothing is more deceptive. How does one distinguish the imaginary from the real in the spiritual domain? One must prefer real hell to imaginary paradise. What distinguishes higher states from lower ones is, in higher states, the coexistence of several superimposed planes. Humility aims to abolish the imaginary in spiritual progress. There is no harm in believing oneself far less advanced than one is: the light operates its effect no less, whose source is not in opinion. There is great harm in believing oneself more advanced, for then opinion has an effect. A criterion of the real is that it is hard and rough. One finds joys in it, not pleasantness. What is pleasant is daydream. To try to love without imagining. To love the bare appearance without interpretation. What one loves then is truly God.

After having passed through the absolute good, one finds again the illusory and partial goods, but in a hierarchical order such that one permits oneself the pursuit of a given good only within the limits allowed by concern for another. This order is transcendent in relation to the goods it connects and is a reflection of the absolute good.

Already discursive reason (the intelligence of relations) helps to dissolve idolatries by considering goods and evils as limited, mixed, and flowing into one another.

To recognize the point where good passes into evil insofar as, to the extent that, with regard to, etc.

To go further than the rule of three.

It is always a matter of a relationship with time. To lose the illusion of possessing time. To become incarnate.

Man must perform the act of becoming incarnate, for he is disincarnated by imagination. What proceeds from Satan in us is imagination.

Remedy against imaginary love. To grant God within oneself the strict minimum, what one absolutely cannot refuse him — and to desire that one day, and as soon as possible, this strict minimum become everything.

Transposition: to believe one is rising because, while keeping the same base inclinations (for example: the desire to prevail over others), one has given them elevated objects.

One would on the contrary rise by attaching elevated inclinations to base objects.

There are prodigies in all passions. A gambler is capable of keeping vigil and fasting almost like a saint; he has premonitions, etc. It is a great danger to love God as a gambler loves gambling. To watch over the level at which one places the infinite. If one places it at the level where only the finite is fitting, it matters little by what name one calls it. The lower parts of myself must love God, but not too much. It would not be God. Let them love as one thirsts and hungers. Only the highest has the right to be satisfied. Fear of God in Saint John of the Cross. Is it not the fear of thinking about God when one is unworthy of it? Of defiling him by thinking of him badly? Through this fear, the lower parts withdraw from God. The flesh is dangerous insofar as it refuses to love God, but also insofar as it indiscreetly meddles in loving him. Why is the will to combat a prejudice a sure sign that one is steeped in it? It necessarily proceeds from an obsession. It constitutes an entirely sterile effort to rid oneself of it. The light of attention in such matters alone is effective, and it is not compatible with a polemical intention. Freudianism as a whole is steeped in the prejudice it sets itself the mission of combating, namely that what is sexual is vile.

There is an essential difference between the mystic who turns toward God the faculty of love and desire whose physiological foundation is sexual energy, and the false imitation of the mystic who, leaving this faculty its natural orientation and giving it an imaginary object, stamps upon that object the label of God's name. The discrimination between these two operations, the second of which is even lower than debauchery, is difficult, but it is possible.

God and the supernatural are hidden and formless in the universe. It is good that they be hidden and nameless in the soul. Otherwise one risks having the imaginary under that name (those who fed and clothed Christ did not know it was Christ). Meaning of the ancient mysteries. Christianity (Catholics and Protestants) speaks too much of holy things.

Morality and literature. Our real life is more than three-quarters composed of imagination and fiction. Rare are true contacts with good and evil.

A science that does not bring us closer to God is worthless.

But if it brings us close to him badly, that is to say to an imaginary God, it is worse...

What nature operates mechanically in me, it is bad to believe I am the author of. But it is even worse to believe the Holy Spirit is the author. That is even further from the truth.

Different types of correlations and passages between contraries:

Through total devotion to a great thing (including God), to give full license within oneself to baseness. Through contemplation of the infinite distance between oneself and what is great, to make the self an instrument of greatness. By what criterion can one distinguish them? The only one, I believe, is that the bad correlation makes unlimited what ought not to be so. Among men (excepting the supreme forms of saintliness and genius), what gives the impression of being true is almost necessarily false, and what is true almost necessarily gives the impression of being false. It takes work to express the true. Also to receive it. One expresses and receives the false, or at least the superficial, without work. When the true seems at least as true as the false, it is the triumph of saintliness or genius. Thus Saint Francis made his listeners weep just as much as a vulgar and theatrical preacher. Duration — whether centuries for civilizations, or years and decades for the individual — has a Darwinian function of eliminating the unfit. What is fit for everything is eternal. In this alone resides the value of what is called experience. But falsehood is an armor by which man often allows the unfit in himself to survive the events that, without this armor, would kill it (thus pride survives humiliations), and this armor is as if secreted by the unfit to ward off danger (pride, in humiliation, thickens the inner falsehood). There is in the soul a kind of phagocytosis; everything that is threatened by time secretes falsehood in order not to die, and in proportion to the danger of death. That is why there is no love of truth without an unreserved consent to death. The cross of Christ is the only gateway to knowledge.

To look upon each sin I have committed as a favor from God. It is a favor that the essential imperfection hidden at the bottom of me has partly manifested itself to my eyes on such a day, at such an hour, in such a circumstance. I desire, I implore that my imperfection manifest itself entirely to my eyes, as much as the gaze of human thought is capable of. Not so that it may be healed, but even if it were never to be healed, so that I may be in the truth.

Everything that is without value flees the light. Here below, one can hide beneath the flesh. At death, one can no longer. One is delivered naked to the light. That is, depending on the case, hell, purgatory, or paradise.

What makes one recoil from efforts that would bring one closer to the good is not the reluctance of the flesh before effort. It is the reluctance of the flesh before the good. For a bad cause, if the stimulus is strong enough, the flesh will accept anything, knowing it can do so without dying. Even death, undergone for a bad cause, is not truly death for the carnal part of the soul. What is mortal for the carnal part of the soul is to see God face to face.

This is why we flee inner emptiness, because God might slip into it.

It is not the pursuit of pleasure and the aversion to effort that produce sin, but the fear of God. One knows that one cannot see him face to face without dying, and one does not want to die. One knows that sin very effectively prevents one from seeing him face to face: pleasure and pain provide us only with the slight push indispensable toward sin, and above all the pretext, the even more indispensable alibi. Just as pretexts are needed for unjust wars, false goods are needed for sin, for one cannot bear the thought of going toward evil. The flesh is not what distances us from God; it is the veil we place before us to screen God from us. Perhaps this is so only from a certain point onward. The image of the cave seems to indicate this. At first it is the movement that hurts. When one reaches the opening, it is the light. Not only does it blind, but it wounds. The eyes revolt against it. Can it be true that from this moment on one can commit only mortal sins? To take the flesh to hide from the light — is that not a mortal sin? Horrible thought. Rather leprosy. I need God to take me by force, for if now death, removing the screen of the flesh, placed me before him face to face, I would flee.

"It is so." In the spiritual life, illusion and truth are distinguished in the same way. What is real in perception and distinguishes it from dreams is not sensations; it is necessity. Distinction between those who remain in the cave, close their eyes, and imagine the journey, and those who make it. Real and imaginary in the spiritual realm too, and there too necessity makes the difference. Not suffering simply, for there are imaginary sufferings. As for inner feeling, nothing is more deceptive. How does one distinguish the imaginary from the real in the spiritual domain? One must prefer real hell to imaginary paradise. What distinguishes higher states from lower ones is, in higher states, the coexistence of several superimposed planes. Humility aims to abolish the imaginary in spiritual progress. There is no harm in believing oneself far less advanced than one is: the light operates its effect no less, whose source is not in opinion. There is great harm in believing oneself more advanced, for then opinion has an effect. A criterion of the real is that it is hard and rough. One finds joys in it, not pleasantness. What is pleasant is daydream. To try to love without imagining. To love the bare appearance without interpretation. What one loves then is truly God.

After having passed through the absolute good, one finds again the illusory and partial goods, but in a hierarchical order such that one permits oneself the pursuit of a given good only within the limits allowed by concern for another. This order is transcendent in relation to the goods it connects and is a reflection of the absolute good.

Already discursive reason (the intelligence of relations) helps to dissolve idolatries by considering goods and evils as limited, mixed, and flowing into one another.

To recognize the point where good passes into evil insofar as, to the extent that, with regard to, etc.

To go further than the rule of three.

It is always a matter of a relationship with time. To lose the illusion of possessing time. To become incarnate.

Man must perform the act of becoming incarnate, for he is disincarnated by imagination. What proceeds from Satan in us is imagination.

Remedy against imaginary love. To grant God within oneself the strict minimum, what one absolutely cannot refuse him — and to desire that one day, and as soon as possible, this strict minimum become everything.

Transposition: to believe one is rising because, while keeping the same base inclinations (for example: the desire to prevail over others), one has given them elevated objects.

One would on the contrary rise by attaching elevated inclinations to base objects.

There are prodigies in all passions. A gambler is capable of keeping vigil and fasting almost like a saint; he has premonitions, etc. It is a great danger to love God as a gambler loves gambling. To watch over the level at which one places the infinite. If one places it at the level where only the finite is fitting, it matters little by what name one calls it. The lower parts of myself must love God, but not too much. It would not be God. Let them love as one thirsts and hungers. Only the highest has the right to be satisfied. Fear of God in Saint John of the Cross. Is it not the fear of thinking about God when one is unworthy of it? Of defiling him by thinking of him badly? Through this fear, the lower parts withdraw from God. The flesh is dangerous insofar as it refuses to love God, but also insofar as it indiscreetly meddles in loving him. Why is the will to combat a prejudice a sure sign that one is steeped in it? It necessarily proceeds from an obsession. It constitutes an entirely sterile effort to rid oneself of it. The light of attention in such matters alone is effective, and it is not compatible with a polemical intention. Freudianism as a whole is steeped in the prejudice it sets itself the mission of combating, namely that what is sexual is vile.

There is an essential difference between the mystic who turns toward God the faculty of love and desire whose physiological foundation is sexual energy, and the false imitation of the mystic who, leaving this faculty its natural orientation and giving it an imaginary object, stamps upon that object the label of God's name. The discrimination between these two operations, the second of which is even lower than debauchery, is difficult, but it is possible.

God and the supernatural are hidden and formless in the universe. It is good that they be hidden and nameless in the soul. Otherwise one risks having the imaginary under that name (those who fed and clothed Christ did not know it was Christ). Meaning of the ancient mysteries. Christianity (Catholics and Protestants) speaks too much of holy things.

Morality and literature. Our real life is more than three-quarters composed of imagination and fiction. Rare are true contacts with good and evil.

A science that does not bring us closer to God is worthless.

But if it brings us close to him badly, that is to say to an imaginary God, it is worse...

What nature operates mechanically in me, it is bad to believe I am the author of. But it is even worse to believe the Holy Spirit is the author. That is even further from the truth.

Different types of correlations and passages between contraries:

Through total devotion to a great thing (including God), to give full license within oneself to baseness. Through contemplation of the infinite distance between oneself and what is great, to make the self an instrument of greatness. By what criterion can one distinguish them? The only one, I believe, is that the bad correlation makes unlimited what ought not to be so. Among men (excepting the supreme forms of saintliness and genius), what gives the impression of being true is almost necessarily false, and what is true almost necessarily gives the impression of being false. It takes work to express the true. Also to receive it. One expresses and receives the false, or at least the superficial, without work. When the true seems at least as true as the false, it is the triumph of saintliness or genius. Thus Saint Francis made his listeners weep just as much as a vulgar and theatrical preacher. Duration — whether centuries for civilizations, or years and decades for the individual — has a Darwinian function of eliminating the unfit. What is fit for everything is eternal. In this alone resides the value of what is called experience. But falsehood is an armor by which man often allows the unfit in himself to survive the events that, without this armor, would kill it (thus pride survives humiliations), and this armor is as if secreted by the unfit to ward off danger (pride, in humiliation, thickens the inner falsehood). There is in the soul a kind of phagocytosis; everything that is threatened by time secretes falsehood in order not to die, and in proportion to the danger of death. That is why there is no love of truth without an unreserved consent to death. The cross of Christ is the only gateway to knowledge.

To look upon each sin I have committed as a favor from God. It is a favor that the essential imperfection hidden at the bottom of me has partly manifested itself to my eyes on such a day, at such an hour, in such a circumstance. I desire, I implore that my imperfection manifest itself entirely to my eyes, as much as the gaze of human thought is capable of. Not so that it may be healed, but even if it were never to be healed, so that I may be in the truth.

Everything that is without value flees the light. Here below, one can hide beneath the flesh. At death, one can no longer. One is delivered naked to the light. That is, depending on the case, hell, purgatory, or paradise.

What makes one recoil from efforts that would bring one closer to the good is not the reluctance of the flesh before effort. It is the reluctance of the flesh before the good. For a bad cause, if the stimulus is strong enough, the flesh will accept anything, knowing it can do so without dying. Even death, undergone for a bad cause, is not truly death for the carnal part of the soul. What is mortal for the carnal part of the soul is to see God face to face.

This is why we flee inner emptiness, because God might slip into it.

It is not the pursuit of pleasure and the aversion to effort that produce sin, but the fear of God. One knows that one cannot see him face to face without dying, and one does not want to die. One knows that sin very effectively prevents one from seeing him face to face: pleasure and pain provide us only with the slight push indispensable toward sin, and above all the pretext, the even more indispensable alibi. Just as pretexts are needed for unjust wars, false goods are needed for sin, for one cannot bear the thought of going toward evil. The flesh is not what distances us from God; it is the veil we place before us to screen God from us. Perhaps this is so only from a certain point onward. The image of the cave seems to indicate this. At first it is the movement that hurts. When one reaches the opening, it is the light. Not only does it blind, but it wounds. The eyes revolt against it. Can it be true that from this moment on one can commit only mortal sins? To take the flesh to hide from the light — is that not a mortal sin? Horrible thought. Rather leprosy. I need God to take me by force, for if now death, removing the screen of the flesh, placed me before him face to face, I would flee.

title: Idolatry
content_html:
Idolatry comes from the fact that, while thirsting for absolute good, one does not possess supernatural attention and has not the patience to let it grow.

Without idols, one must often, every day or nearly so, toil in a void. One cannot do this without supernatural bread.

Idolatry is therefore a vital necessity in the cave. Even among the best, it inevitably narrows intelligence and goodness.

Thoughts are changeable, obedient to passions, to whims, to fatigue. Activity must be continuous, every day, many hours a day. One therefore needs motives for activity that escape thoughts, and thus escape relations: idols.

All men are ready to die for what they love. They differ only in the level of the thing loved and the concentration or dispersion of their love. None loves himself.

Man would like to be selfish and cannot. This is the most striking feature of his wretchedness and the source of his greatness.

Man always devotes himself to an order. Only, barring supernatural illumination, this order has as its center either himself or a particular being (which may be an abstraction) into which he has transferred himself (Napoleon for his soldiers, Science, the Party, etc.). Perspectival order. We do not have to acquire humility. Humility is in us. Only we humble ourselves before false gods.

title: Love
content_html:
Love is a sign of our wretchedness. God can love only himself. We can love only something other than ourselves.

It is not because God loves us that we must love him. It is because God loves us that we must love ourselves. How could one love oneself without this motive?

Self-love is impossible for man, except by this detour.

If my eyes are bandaged and my hands chained to a stick, this stick separates me from things, but through it I explore them. I feel only the stick, I perceive only the wall. Likewise creatures for the faculty of love. Supernatural love touches only creatures and goes only to God. It loves only creatures (what else do we have to love?) but as intermediaries. In this respect, it loves all creatures equally, including oneself. To love a stranger as oneself implies as its counterpart: to love oneself as a stranger.

The love of God is pure when joy and suffering inspire an equal gratitude.

Love, in one who is happy, is to wish to share the suffering of the beloved who is unhappy.

Love, in one who is unhappy, is to be filled by the simple knowledge that the beloved is in joy, without sharing in that joy, nor even desiring to share in it.

In the eyes of Plato, carnal love is a degraded image of true love. Chaste human love (conjugal fidelity) is a less degraded image. The idea of sublimation could only have arisen in contemporary stupidity. Love of the Phaedrus. It neither exercises nor undergoes force. Therein lies the only purity. Contact with the sword carries the same defilement, whether from the side of the hilt or from the side of the blade. For one who loves, the cold of metal will not take away the love, but will give the feeling of being abandoned by God. Supernatural love has no contact with force, but neither does it protect the soul against the cold of force, the cold of iron. Only an earthly attachment, if it contains enough energy, can protect against the cold of iron. Armor is made of metal like the sword. For one who loves only with a pure love, murder chills the soul, whether one is its author or its victim, and everything that, without going as far as death itself, is violence. If one desires a love that protects the soul against wounds, one must love something other than God. Love tends to go ever further. But it has a limit. When the limit is exceeded, love turns to hatred. To avoid this transformation, love must become other. Among human beings, one fully recognizes the existence only of those one loves. The belief in the existence of other human beings as such is love. The mind is not compelled to believe in the existence of anything (subjectivism, absolute idealism, solipsism, skepticism: see the Upanishads, the Taoists, and Plato, who all use this philosophical attitude as a purification). That is why the only organ of contact with existence is acceptance, love. That is why beauty and reality are identical. That is why joy and the feeling of reality are identical. This need to be the creator of what one loves is a need to imitate God. But it is an inclination toward false divinity. Unless one has recourse to the model seen from the other side of heaven... Pure love of creatures: not love in God, but love that has passed through God as through fire. Love that detaches itself completely from creatures in order to ascend to God and descends again from him joined to the creative love of God. Thus are united the two contraries that tear human love apart: to love the beloved as he is and to wish to recreate him. Imaginary love for creatures. One is attached by a cord to all objects of attachment, and a cord can always be cut. One is also attached by a cord to the imaginary God, to the God for whom love is also attachment. But to the real God one is not attached, and that is why there is no cord that can be cut. He enters into us. He alone can enter into us. All other things remain outside, and we know of them only the tensions of varying degree and direction impressed upon the cord when there is movement of them or of us. Love needs reality. To love through a bodily appearance an imaginary being — what could be more atrocious, the day one realizes it? Far more atrocious than death, for death does not prevent the beloved from having existed.

It is the punishment for the crime of having fed love with imagination. It is a cowardice to seek from the people one loves (or to desire to give them) any other comfort than that which works of art give us, helping us by the simple fact that they exist. To love, to be loved — this only makes that existence more concrete, more constantly present to the mind. But it must be present as the source of thoughts, not as their object. If there is reason to desire to be understood, it is not for oneself, but for the other, in order to exist for that person. Everything that is vile or mediocre in us revolts against purity and needs, to save its life, to defile that purity. To defile is to modify, to touch. The beautiful is what one cannot wish to change. To take power over is to defile. To possess is to defile. To love purely is to consent to distance, to adore the distance between oneself and what one loves. Imagination is always linked to a desire, that is, to a value. Only desire without an object is empty of imagination. There is real presence of God in everything that imagination does not veil. The beautiful captures the desire in us and empties it of its object by giving it a present object and thereby forbidding it to rush toward the future. Such is the price of chaste love. Every desire for enjoyment is situated in the future, in the illusory. Whereas if one desires only that a being exist, that being exists: what more then could one desire? The beloved is then naked and real, not veiled by an imaginary future. The miser never looks at his treasure without imagining it n times larger. One must be dead to see things naked.

Thus, in love, there is chastity or lack of chastity according to whether the desire is directed or not toward the future.

In this sense, and provided it is not directed toward a pseudo-immortality conceived on the model of the future, the love one bears the dead is perfectly pure. For it is the desire for a finite life that can no longer give anything new. One desires that the dead person existed, and he did exist.

Where the mind ceases to be a principle, it ceases also to be an end. Hence the rigorous connection between collective "thought" in all its forms and the loss of the sense of, and respect for, souls. The soul is the human being considered as having a value in himself. To love a woman's soul is not to think of that woman in terms of one's own pleasure, etc. Love no longer knows how to contemplate; it wants to possess (disappearance of Platonic love).

It is a fault to desire to be understood before having elucidated oneself in one's own eyes. It is to seek pleasures in friendship, and undeserved ones. It is something even more corrupting than love. You would sell your soul for friendship.

Learn to reject friendship, or rather the dream of friendship. To desire friendship is a great fault. Friendship must be a gratuitous joy like those given by art or by life. One must refuse it in order to be worthy of receiving it: it belongs to the order of grace ("My God, withdraw from me..."). It is among those things that are given as a bonus. Every dream of friendship deserves to be shattered. It is not by chance that you have never been loved... To desire to escape from solitude is a cowardice. Friendship is not sought, not dreamed of, not desired; it is exercised (it is a virtue). Abolish all that margin of feeling, impure and turbid. Enough! Or rather (for one must not prune oneself too rigorously), everything in friendship that does not pass into actual exchanges must pass into considered thoughts. It is quite useless to do without the inspiring virtue of friendship. What must be severely forbidden is to dream of the pleasures of sentiment. That is corruption. And it is as stupid as dreaming about music or painting. Friendship does not let itself be detached from reality, any more than the beautiful does. It constitutes a miracle, like the beautiful. And the miracle consists simply in the fact that it exists. At twenty-five, it is high time to finish radically with adolescence... Do not let yourself be imprisoned by any affection. Preserve your solitude. The day, should it ever come, when a true affection would be given to you, there would be no opposition between inner solitude and friendship; on the contrary. It is even by this infallible sign that you would recognize it. Other affections must be severely disciplined. The same words (for example, a man says to his wife: I love you) can be vulgar or extraordinary depending on the manner in which they are spoken. And this manner depends on the depth of the region of being from which they proceed, without the will being able to do anything about it. And, by a marvelous accord, they go to touch, in the listener, the same region. Thus the listener can discern, if he has discernment, the worth of these words. Beneficence is permitted precisely because it constitutes a humiliation even greater than pain, a still more intimate and irrefutable trial of dependence. And gratitude is prescribed for this reason, because this is the use to be made of the benefit received. But it must be dependence on fate and not on a particular human being. That is why the benefactor has the obligation to be entirely absent from the benefit. And gratitude must not to any degree constitute an attachment, for that is the gratitude of dogs. Gratitude belongs first to the one who gives help, if the help is pure. It is owed by the recipient only as reciprocity. To feel pure gratitude (the case of friendship being set aside), I need to think that I am well treated not out of pity, or sympathy, or caprice, as a favor or privilege, nor by a natural effect of temperament, but out of a desire to do what justice requires. Therefore the one who treats me thus wishes that all who are in my situation be treated thus by all who are in his.

title: Evil
content_html:
Creation: the good broken into pieces and scattered throughout evil. Evil is the limitless, but it is not infinite. Only the infinite limits the limitless. Monotony of evil: nothing new; everything in it is equivalent. Nothing real; everything in it is imaginary. It is because of this monotony that quantity plays such a great role. Many women (Celimene), or men (Don Juan), etc. Condemned to false infinity. Therein lies hell itself. Evil is license, and that is why it is monotonous: everything must be drawn from oneself. But man is not given the power to create. It is a bad attempt to imitate God. Not to know and accept this impossibility of creating is the source of many errors. We must imitate the act of creating, and there are two possible imitations — one real, the other apparent — to preserve and to destroy. No trace of "I" in preservation. There is in destruction. "I" leaves its mark on the world by destroying. Literature and morality. Imaginary evil is romantic, varied; real evil is dreary, monotonous, barren, boring. Imaginary good is boring; real good is always new, marvelous, intoxicating. Therefore "imaginative literature" is either boring or immoral (or a mixture of the two). It escapes this alternative only by passing, as it were, by sheer force of art, to the side of reality — which only genius can do.

A certain inferior virtue is a degraded image of good, of which one must repent, and of which it is harder to repent than of evil. Pharisee and publican.

Good as the contrary of evil is in a sense equivalent to it, like all contraries.

What evil violates is not the good, for the good is inviolable; one violates only a degraded good.

What is directly contrary to an evil is never of the order of the higher good. Barely above evil, often! Examples: theft and bourgeois respect for property; adultery and "respectable woman"; savings account and squandering; lying and "sincerity."

Good is essentially other than evil. Evil is multiple and fragmentary; good is one. Evil is apparent; good is mysterious. Evil consists in actions; good in non-action, in non-acting action, etc. Good taken at the level of evil and opposing it as a contrary to a contrary is a good of the penal code. Above this is a good that, in a sense, resembles evil more than it resembles this low form of good. This makes possible much demagoguery and tedious paradox.

The good that defines itself in the way one defines evil must be denied. Now evil denies it. But it denies it badly.

Is there a union of incompatible vices in beings devoted to evil? I do not think so. Vices are subject to gravity, and that is why there is no depth, no transcendence in evil. One has the experience of good only by accomplishing it. One has the experience of evil only by forbidding oneself to accomplish it, or, if one has accomplished it, by repenting. When one accomplishes evil, one does not know it, because evil flees the light. Does evil, as one conceives it when one does not do it, exist? Does not the evil one does seem something simple, natural, self-evident? Is not evil analogous to illusion? Illusion, when one is its victim, is not felt as an illusion, but as a reality. Likewise, perhaps, evil. Evil, when one is in it, is not felt as evil, but as necessity, or even as duty. As soon as one does evil, evil appears as a kind of duty. Most people have a sense of duty in certain bad things and other good ones. The same man feels it a duty to sell as dearly as he can and not to steal, etc. The good in them is at the level of evil, a good without light. The sensibility of the innocent who suffers is like sensible crime. True crime is not sensible. The innocent who suffers knows the truth about his torturer; the torturer does not know it. The evil that the innocent feels within himself is in his torturer, but there it is not felt. What in the criminal is not felt is the crime. What in the innocent is not felt is the innocence. It is the innocent who can feel hell. The sin that is in us goes out of us and spreads outward, exerting a contagion in the form of sin. Thus when we are irritated, those around us become irritated. Or again, from superior to inferior: anger provokes fear. But at the contact of a perfectly pure being, there is transmutation, and sin becomes suffering. Such is the function of the just one of Isaiah, of the lamb of God. Such is redemptive suffering. All the criminal violence of the Roman Empire struck against Christ, and in him became pure suffering. Evil beings, on the contrary, transform simple suffering (for example, illness) into sin. It follows perhaps that redemptive suffering must be of social origin. It must be injustice, violence exercised by human beings. The false God changes suffering into violence. The true God changes violence into suffering. Expiatory suffering is the backlash of the evil one has done. And redemptive suffering is the shadow of the pure good one desires. The wicked act is a transfer onto another of the degradation one carries within oneself. That is why one inclines toward it as toward a deliverance. Every crime is a transfer of evil from the one who acts to the one who suffers it. Illegitimate love, like murder. The apparatus of criminal justice has been so contaminated by evil for centuries, through contact with criminals without compensating purification, that a conviction is very often a transfer of evil from the penal apparatus to the condemned, even if he is guilty and even if the penalty is not disproportionate. Hardened criminals are the only ones on whom the penal apparatus can do no harm. On the innocent, it does terrible harm. When there is a transfer of evil, evil is not diminished but increased in the one from whom it proceeds. A phenomenon of multiplication. The same is true of the transfer of evil onto objects. Then where to put evil? One must transfer it from the impure part into the pure part of oneself, thus transmuting it into pure suffering. The crime that is in oneself, one must inflict it on oneself. But one would quickly defile the point of inner purity in this way if one did not renew it through contact with an inalterable purity placed beyond all reach. Patience consists in not transforming suffering into crime. This alone is enough to transform crime into suffering. To transfer evil onto external things is to deform the relations of things. What is exact and determinate — number, proportion, harmony — resists this deformation. Whatever my state of vigor or weariness, in five kilometers there are five milestones. That is why number hurts when one suffers: it opposes the operation of transfer. To fix one's attention on what is too rigorous to be deformed by one's inner modifications is to prepare within oneself the appearance of an invariant and access to the eternal.

To accept the evil done to us as a remedy for the evil we have done. It is not the suffering one imposes on oneself, but the suffering one undergoes from outside that is the true remedy. And moreover, it must be unjust. When one has sinned through injustice, it is not enough to suffer justly; one must suffer injustice. Purity is absolutely invulnerable as purity, in the sense that no violence makes it less pure. But it is eminently vulnerable in the sense that any touch of evil makes it suffer, that any sin that touches it becomes suffering within it. If someone does me harm, to desire that this harm not degrade, out of love for the one who inflicts it, so that he may not truly have done harm. The saints (the near-saints) are more exposed than others to the devil, because the real knowledge they have of their wretchedness makes the light almost intolerable to them. The sin against the Spirit consists in knowing a thing as good and hating it as good. One experiences the equivalent of it in the form of resistance every time one turns toward the good. For every contact with the good produces a knowledge of the distance between evil and good and a beginning of painful effort of assimilation. It is a pain, and one is afraid. This fear is perhaps the sign of the reality of the contact. The corresponding sin can only occur if a lack of hope makes the consciousness of the distance intolerable and changes pain into hatred. Hope is a remedy in this regard. But a better remedy is indifference to oneself, and to be glad that the good is the good, even though one is far from it, and even on the supposition that one were destined to move infinitely farther from it.

Once an atom of pure good has entered the soul, the greatest, most criminal weakness is infinitely less dangerous than the slightest betrayal, even if this betrayal were reduced to a purely interior movement of thought, lasting only an instant, but consented to. It is participation in hell. As long as the soul has not tasted pure good, it is separated from hell as from paradise.

An infernal choice is possible only through attachment to salvation. Whoever does not desire the joy of God but is satisfied to know that there is real joy in God falls but does not betray.

When one loves God through evil as such, it is truly God that one loves.

To love God through evil as such. To love God through the evil that one hates, while hating that evil. To love God as the author of the evil one is in the act of hating.

Evil is to love what mystery is to intelligence. As mystery compels the virtue of faith to be supernatural, so does evil for the virtue of charity. And trying to find compensations for, justifications of evil is as harmful to charity as trying to set forth the content of mysteries on the plane of human intelligence.

Ivan's speech in the Karamazovs: "Even if this vast factory were to produce the most extraordinary marvels and cost only a single tear of a single child, I refuse."

I adhere completely to this sentiment. No motive of any kind that could be given me to compensate for a child's tear can make me accept that tear. None at all that the intelligence can conceive. Only one, but one that is intelligible only to supernatural love: God willed it. And for this motive I would accept a world that were nothing but evil just as readily as a child's tear. The agony is the supreme dark night of which even the perfect have need for absolute purity, and for this it is better that it be bitter. The unreality that removes good from good — that is what constitutes evil. Evil is always the destruction of sensible things in which there is a real presence of good. Evil is accomplished by those who have no knowledge of this real presence. In this sense it is true that no one is willingly wicked. The relations of force give absence the power to destroy presence. One cannot contemplate without terror the extent of the evil that man can do and suffer. How could one believe it possible to find a compensation for this evil, since because of this evil God suffered the crucifixion? Good and evil. Reality. What is good is what gives more reality to beings and things; what is evil is what takes it from them. The Romans did evil in stripping Greek cities of their statues, because the cities, the temples, the life of those Greeks had less reality without the statues, and because the statues could not have as much reality in Rome as in Greece.

The desperate, humble supplications of the Greeks to keep a few statues: a desperate attempt to convey to the mind of another one's own notion of values. Understood in this way, it has nothing base about it. But it is almost necessarily ineffective. The duty to understand and weigh the system of values of another, together with one's own, on the same scale. To forge the scale. To let one's imagination dwell on what is evil implies a kind of cowardice; one hopes to enjoy, to know, and to grow through the unreal. Even to dwell in imagination on certain things as possible (which is something quite different from clearly conceiving their possibility, an essential thing for virtue) is already to commit oneself. Curiosity is the cause of it. To forbid oneself (not to conceive, but to dwell on) certain thoughts; not to think about. One believes that thought does not commit, but thought alone commits, and the license to think contains every license. Not to think about — the supreme faculty. Purity, a negative virtue. Having dwelt in imagination on a bad thing, if one meets other people who make it objective through their words and actions and thus remove the social barrier, one is already nearly lost. And what could be easier? There is no breaking point; when one sees the ditch, one has already crossed it. For the good, it is the exact opposite; the ditch is seen when it is to be crossed, at the moment of tearing away and rending. One does not fall into the good. The word baseness expresses this property of evil. Even once accomplished, evil retains this character of unreality; hence perhaps the simplicity of criminals — everything is simple in a dream. A simplicity that parallels that of the highest virtue.

Evil must be made pure — or life is impossible. God alone can do this. This is the idea of the Gita. It is also the idea of Moses, of Muhammad, of Hitlerism... But Jehovah, Allah, Hitler are earthly gods. The purification they accomplish is imaginary. What is essentially other than evil is virtue accompanied by a clear perception of the possibility of evil, of evil appearing as a good. The presence of illusions abandoned but held present to thought is perhaps the criterion of truth. One cannot have horror of harming others unless one has reached the point where others can no longer harm us (one then loves others, at the limit, as one's own past self). The contemplation of human wretchedness tears one toward God, and it is only in others loved as oneself that one contemplates it. One cannot contemplate it either in oneself as such or in others as such. Extreme affliction that seizes human beings does not create human wretchedness; it only reveals it. Sin and the prestige of force. From the fact that the whole soul has not been able to know and accept human wretchedness, one believes there is a difference between human beings, and thereby one fails in justice, either by making a distinction between ourselves and others, or by showing favoritism among others. This comes from not knowing that human wretchedness is a constant and irreducible quantity, as great in every man as it can be, and that greatness comes from a single God, so that there is identity between one man and another. One is surprised that affliction does not ennoble. That is because when one thinks of an afflicted person, one thinks of his affliction. But the afflicted person does not think of his affliction: his soul is filled with any insignificant relief he can covet. How could there not be evil in the world? The world must be foreign to our desires. If it were foreign to them without containing evil, then our desires would be entirely bad. That must not be so. There are all degrees of distance between the creature and God. A distance at which love of God is impossible. Matter, plants, animals. Evil is so complete there that it destroys itself; there is no longer any evil: mirror of divine innocence. We are at the point where love is just barely possible. It is a great privilege, for the love that unites is proportional to the distance. God created a world that is not the best possible, but one that contains all degrees of good and of evil. We are at the point where it is the worst possible. For beyond is the degree where evil becomes innocence.

title: Affliction
content_html:
Suffering: the superiority of man over God. The Incarnation was necessary so that this superiority would not be scandalous. I must not love my suffering because it is useful, but because it is. To accept what is bitter; the acceptance must not reflect back upon the bitterness and diminish it, otherwise the acceptance diminishes proportionally in strength and purity. For the object of acceptance is what is bitter insofar as it is bitter and nothing else. — To say, like Ivan Karamazov: nothing can compensate for a single tear of a single child. And yet to accept all the tears, and the innumerable horrors that lie beyond tears. To accept these things, not insofar as they might entail compensations, but in themselves. To accept that they are simply because they are. If there were no affliction in this world, we could believe ourselves in paradise. Two conceptions of hell. The ordinary one (suffering without consolation); mine (false beatitude, believing by error that one is in paradise). Greater purity of physical pain (Thibon). Hence, greater dignity of the common people. Not to seek not to suffer or to suffer less, but not to be altered by suffering.

The extreme greatness of Christianity comes from the fact that it does not seek a supernatural remedy against suffering, but a supernatural use of suffering. One must strive as much as possible to avoid affliction, so that the affliction one encounters may be perfectly pure and perfectly bitter. Joy is the fullness of the feeling of reality. But to suffer while preserving the feeling of reality is better. To suffer without sinking into nightmare. Let pain be, in one sense purely external, in another sense purely internal. For this, it must reside in the sensibility alone. It is then external (as being outside the spiritual parts of the soul) and internal (as concentrated entirely upon ourselves, without reflecting back on the universe to alter it). Affliction forces one to recognize as real what one does not believe possible. Affliction: time carries the thinking being against his will toward what he cannot bear and which will come nonetheless. "Let this cup pass from me." Each second that passes carries a being in the world toward something he cannot bear. There is a point of affliction where one is no longer capable of bearing either that it continue or of being delivered from it. Suffering is nothing, apart from the relation between past and future, but what is more real for man than this relation? It is reality itself. Future. One thinks it will come tomorrow until the moment one thinks it will never come.

Two thoughts lighten affliction somewhat. Either that it will cease almost immediately or that it will never cease. Impossible or necessary. But one cannot think that it simply is. That is unbearable. "It is not possible." What is not possible is to think of a future in which affliction would continue. The natural impulse of thought toward the future is halted, the being is torn in his feeling of time. "In a month, in a year, how shall we suffer?" The being who can bear to think neither of the past nor of the future: he is brought down to the level of matter. White Russians at Renault. One can thus learn to obey like matter, but doubtless they fabricated for themselves near and false pasts and futures. Fragmentation of time for criminals and prostitutes; it is the same for slaves. This is therefore a characteristic of affliction. Time commits violence; it is the only violence. Another shall gird you and carry you where you do not wish to go; time carries us where we do not wish to go. Let me be condemned to death, I shall not be executed if, in the interval, time stops. Whatever terrible thing may happen, can one desire that time should stop, that the stars should stop? The violence of time tears the soul: through the tear enters eternity. All problems come down to time. Extreme pain: time without direction: the way to hell or to paradise. Perpetuity or eternity. It is not joy and pain that are opposed, but the species of each. There is an infernal joy and an infernal pain, a healing joy and a healing pain, a celestial joy and a celestial pain. By nature, we flee suffering and seek pleasure. It is solely in this respect that joy serves as an image of the good and pain as an image of evil. Hence the imagery of paradise and hell. But in fact, pleasure and pain are inseparable couples. Suffering, teaching, and transformation. What is needed is not that the initiates learn something, but that a transformation take place in them which renders them apt to receive the teaching. Pathos means both suffering (especially suffering unto death) and modification (especially transformation into an immortal being). Suffering and enjoyment as sources of knowledge. The serpent offered knowledge to Adam and Eve. The sirens offered knowledge to Ulysses. These stories teach that the soul is lost in seeking knowledge through pleasure. Why? Pleasure is perhaps innocent, provided one does not seek knowledge in it. It is permitted to seek knowledge only in suffering. The infinite that is in man is at the mercy of a small piece of iron; such is the human condition; space and time are the cause. It is impossible to handle this piece of iron without abruptly reducing the infinite that is in man to a point at the tip, a point at the handle, at the price of a tearing pain. The entire being is affected for a moment; there remains in it no room for God, even in Christ, where the thought of God is no longer at least anything but that of a deprivation. One must reach that point for there to be incarnation.

The entire being becomes deprivation of God; how can one go further? There is nothing after that but the resurrection. To go that far, one needs the cold contact of naked iron. One must, at the contact of iron, feel separated from God as Christ did, otherwise it is another God. The martyrs did not feel separated from God, but it was another God, and it was perhaps better not to be a martyr. The God in whom the martyrs found joy in tortures or death is close to the one who was officially adopted by the Empire and then imposed through exterminations. To say that the world is worth nothing, that this life is worth nothing, and to offer evil as proof, is absurd, for if it is worth nothing, of what does evil deprive us? Thus suffering in affliction and compassion for others are all the purer and more intense the better one conceives the fullness of joy. Of what does suffering deprive the one who is without joy? And if one conceives the fullness of joy, suffering is to joy as hunger is to food. One must have had, through joy, the revelation of reality in order to find reality in suffering. Otherwise life is only a more or less bad dream. One must manage to find a reality even fuller in suffering, which is nothingness and void. Likewise one must love life greatly to love death still more.
content_text:
Suffering: the superiority of man over God. The Incarnation was necessary so that this superiority would not be scandalous. I must not love my suffering because it is useful, but because it is. To accept what is bitter; the acceptance must not reflect back upon the bitterness and diminish it, otherwise the acceptance diminishes proportionally in strength and purity. For the object of acceptance is what is bitter insofar as it is bitter and nothing else. — To say, like Ivan Karamazov: nothing can compensate for a single tear of a single child. And yet to accept all the tears, and the innumerable horrors that lie beyond tears. To accept these things, not insofar as they might entail compensations, but in themselves. To accept that they are simply because they are. If there were no affliction in this world, we could believe ourselves in paradise. Two conceptions of hell. The ordinary one (suffering without consolation); mine (false beatitude, believing by error that one is in paradise). Greater purity of physical pain (Thibon). Hence, greater dignity of the common people. Not to seek not to suffer or to suffer less, but not to be altered by suffering.

The extreme greatness of Christianity comes from the fact that it does not seek a supernatural remedy against suffering, but a supernatural use of suffering. One must strive as much as possible to avoid affliction, so that the affliction one encounters may be perfectly pure and perfectly bitter. Joy is the fullness of the feeling of reality. But to suffer while preserving the feeling of reality is better. To suffer without sinking into nightmare. Let pain be, in one sense purely external, in another sense purely internal. For this, it must reside in the sensibility alone. It is then external (as being outside the spiritual parts of the soul) and internal (as concentrated entirely upon ourselves, without reflecting back on the universe to alter it). Affliction forces one to recognize as real what one does not believe possible. Affliction: time carries the thinking being against his will toward what he cannot bear and which will come nonetheless. "Let this cup pass from me." Each second that passes carries a being in the world toward something he cannot bear. There is a point of affliction where one is no longer capable of bearing either that it continue or of being delivered from it. Suffering is nothing, apart from the relation between past and future, but what is more real for man than this relation? It is reality itself. Future. One thinks it will come tomorrow until the moment one thinks it will never come.

Two thoughts lighten affliction somewhat. Either that it will cease almost immediately or that it will never cease. Impossible or necessary. But one cannot think that it simply is. That is unbearable. "It is not possible." What is not possible is to think of a future in which affliction would continue. The natural impulse of thought toward the future is halted, the being is torn in his feeling of time. "In a month, in a year, how shall we suffer?" The being who can bear to think neither of the past nor of the future: he is brought down to the level of matter. White Russians at Renault. One can thus learn to obey like matter, but doubtless they fabricated for themselves near and false pasts and futures. Fragmentation of time for criminals and prostitutes; it is the same for slaves. This is therefore a characteristic of affliction. Time commits violence; it is the only violence. Another shall gird you and carry you where you do not wish to go; time carries us where we do not wish to go. Let me be condemned to death, I shall not be executed if, in the interval, time stops. Whatever terrible thing may happen, can one desire that time should stop, that the stars should stop? The violence of time tears the soul: through the tear enters eternity. All problems come down to time. Extreme pain: time without direction: the way to hell or to paradise. Perpetuity or eternity. It is not joy and pain that are opposed, but the species of each. There is an infernal joy and an infernal pain, a healing joy and a healing pain, a celestial joy and a celestial pain. By nature, we flee suffering and seek pleasure. It is solely in this respect that joy serves as an image of the good and pain as an image of evil. Hence the imagery of paradise and hell. But in fact, pleasure and pain are inseparable couples. Suffering, teaching, and transformation. What is needed is not that the initiates learn something, but that a transformation take place in them which renders them apt to receive the teaching. Pathos means both suffering (especially suffering unto death) and modification (especially transformation into an immortal being). Suffering and enjoyment as sources of knowledge. The serpent offered knowledge to Adam and Eve. The sirens offered knowledge to Ulysses. These stories teach that the soul is lost in seeking knowledge through pleasure. Why? Pleasure is perhaps innocent, provided one does not seek knowledge in it. It is permitted to seek knowledge only in suffering. The infinite that is in man is at the mercy of a small piece of iron; such is the human condition; space and time are the cause. It is impossible to handle this piece of iron without abruptly reducing the infinite that is in man to a point at the tip, a point at the handle, at the price of a tearing pain. The entire being is affected for a moment; there remains in it no room for God, even in Christ, where the thought of God is no longer at least anything but that of a deprivation. One must reach that point for there to be incarnation.

The entire being becomes deprivation of God; how can one go further? There is nothing after that but the resurrection. To go that far, one needs the cold contact of naked iron. One must, at the contact of iron, feel separated from God as Christ did, otherwise it is another God. The martyrs did not feel separated from God, but it was another God, and it was perhaps better not to be a martyr. The God in whom the martyrs found joy in tortures or death is close to the one who was officially adopted by the Empire and then imposed through exterminations. title: Violence
content_html:
Death is what has been given most precious to man. That is why the supreme impiety is to make bad use of it. To die badly. To kill badly. (But how can one escape both suicide and murder?) After death, love. An analogous problem: neither bad enjoyment nor bad privation. War and Eros are the two sources of illusion and falsehood among men. Their mixture is the greatest impurity. To strive to substitute increasingly in the world effective non-violence for violence. Non-violence is good only if it is effective. Thus, the question of the young man to Gandhi concerning his sister. The answer should be: use force, unless you are such that you can defend her, with an equal probability of success, without violence. Unless you possess a radiance whose energy (that is, whose possible efficacy, in the most material sense) is equal to that contained in your muscles. To strive to become such that one can be non-violent. This also depends on the adversary. The cause of wars: each man, each human group, feels itself rightly the legitimate master and possessor of the universe. But this possession is poorly understood, for want of knowing that access to it — insofar as it is possible for man on earth — passes, for each person, through his own body.

Alexander is to a peasant landowner what Don Juan is to a happy husband. War. To keep intact within oneself the love of life; never to inflict death without accepting it for oneself. In the case where the life of X... were linked to one's own to the point that the two deaths must be simultaneous, would one still wish him to die? If body and soul in their entirety aspire to life and yet, without lying, one can answer yes, then one has the right to kill.

title: The Cross
content_html:
Whoever takes up the sword shall perish by the sword. And whoever does not take up the sword (or lets it go) shall perish on the cross. Christ healing the infirm, raising the dead, etc. — that is the humble, human, almost lowly part of his mission. The supernatural part is the sweat of blood, the unsatisfied desire for human consolation, the supplication to be spared, the feeling of being abandoned by God. The abandonment at the supreme moment of the crucifixion, what an abyss of love on both sides! "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" There is the true proof that Christianity is something divine. To be just, one must be naked and dead. Without imagination. That is why the model of justice must be naked and dead. The cross alone is not susceptible of imaginary imitation. A just man is needed to imitate so that the imitation of God may not be a mere word, but it is necessary, in order that we may be carried beyond the will, that we cannot will to imitate him. One cannot will the cross. One could will any degree of asceticism or heroism, but not the choice which is penal suffering. Those who conceive of the crucifixion only as an offering erase its saving mystery and its saving bitterness.

To wish for martyrdom is far too little. The cross is infinitely more than martyrdom. The most purely bitter suffering, penal suffering, as a guarantee of authenticity. Cross. The tree of sin was a real tree, the tree of life was a beam. Something that bears no fruit, but only vertical movement. "The Son of Man must be lifted up, and he will draw you to himself." One can kill in oneself the vital energy while preserving only the vertical movement. Leaves and fruit are a waste of energy if one wishes only to ascend. Eve and Adam wanted to seek divinity in vital energy. A tree, a fruit. But it is prepared for us on geometrically squared dead wood on which hangs a corpse. The secret of our kinship with God must be sought in our mortality. God exhausts himself, across the infinite thickness of time and space, to reach the soul and seduce it. If it allows itself to be wrested, were it only for the duration of a flash of lightning, a pure and entire consent, then God conquers it. And when it has become a thing entirely his, he abandons it. He leaves it completely alone. And it must in its turn, but groping, traverse the infinite thickness of time and space, in search of the one it loves. Thus the soul retraces in reverse the journey God made toward it. And that is the cross. God is crucified by the fact that finite beings, subject to necessity, to space, and to time, think. To know that as a thinking and finite being, I am God crucified.

To resemble God, but God crucified. God almighty insofar as he is bound by necessity. Prometheus, the god crucified for having loved men too much. Hippolytus, the man punished for having been too pure and too loved by the gods. It is the bringing together of the human and the divine that calls down punishment. We are what is farthest from God, at the extreme limit from which it is not absolutely impossible to return to him. In our being, God is torn. We are the crucifixion of God. The love of God for us is passion. How could the good love evil without suffering? And evil also suffers in loving the good. The mutual love of God and man is suffering. For us to feel the distance between ourselves and God, God must be a crucified slave. For we feel distance only downward. It is much easier to put oneself by imagination in the place of God the creator than in the place of the crucified Christ. The dimensions of the charity of Christ are the distance between God and the creature. The function of mediation, in itself, implies being torn apart... That is why one cannot conceive of God's descent toward man or man's ascent toward God without being torn apart. We have to traverse — and God first, to come to us, for he comes first — the infinite thickness of time and space. In the relations between God and man, love is the greatest. It is as great as the distance to be crossed. For love to be as great as possible, the distance must be as great as possible. That is why evil can go to the extreme limit beyond which the very possibility of good would vanish. It is licensed to touch that limit. It sometimes seems that it exceeds it. This is in a sense exactly the opposite of Leibniz's thought. It is certainly more compatible with the greatness of God, for if he had made the best of all possible worlds, it is because he could do little. God traverses the thickness of the world to come to us. The Passion is the existence of perfect justice without any admixture of appearance. Justice is essentially non-acting. It must be either transcendent or suffering. It is purely supernatural justice, absolutely deprived of every sensible support, even the love of God insofar as it is sensible. Redemptive suffering is that which strips suffering bare and carries it in its purity to the point of existence. That saves existence. As God is present in the sensory perception of a piece of bread through the Eucharistic consecration, he is present in extreme evil through redemptive suffering, through the cross. From human misery to God. But not as compensation or consolation. As correlation.

There are people for whom everything that brings God closer to them is beneficial. For me, it is everything that distances him. Between me and him, the thickness of the universe — and that of the cross added to it. Pain is at once entirely external and entirely essential to innocence. Blood on snow. Innocence and evil. Let evil itself be pure. It can be pure only in the form of the suffering of an innocent. An innocent who suffers spreads over evil the light of salvation. He is the visible image of the innocent God. That is why a God who loves man, a man who loves God, must suffer. Happy innocence. Something also infinitely precious. But it is a precarious happiness, fragile, a happiness of chance. Apple blossoms. Happiness is not bound to innocence. To be innocent is to bear the weight of the entire universe. It is to throw the counterweight. In emptying oneself, one exposes oneself to all the pressure of the surrounding universe. God gives himself to men as powerful or as perfect — at their choice.

title: Balance and Lever
content_html:
Cross as balance, as lever. Descent, condition of the ascent. Heaven descending to earth raises earth to heaven. Lever. To lower when one wishes to raise. It is in the same manner that "he who humbles himself shall be exalted." There is also a necessity and laws in the domain of grace. "Even hell has its laws" (Goethe). Heaven too. A rigorous necessity that excludes all arbitrariness, all chance, governs material phenomena. There is, if possible, even less arbitrariness and chance in spiritual things, though free. One, the smallest of numbers. "The one which is the only wise." It is the infinite. A number that grows thinks it draws near to the infinite. It moves away from it. One must lower oneself to rise. If 1 is God, infinity is the devil. Human misery contains the secret of divine wisdom, and not pleasure. Every pursuit of pleasure is pursuit of an artificial paradise, of an intoxication, of an increase. But it gives us nothing, except the experience that it is vain. Only the contemplation of our limits and our misery places us on a plane above. "He who humbles himself shall be exalted."

The upward movement in us is vain (and worse than vain) if it does not proceed from a downward movement. Statera facta corporis. It is the crucified body that is a just balance, the body reduced to its point in time and space. Not to judge. In the manner of the Father in heaven who does not judge: through him beings judge themselves. To let all beings come to oneself, and let them judge themselves. To be a balance. One will not be judged then, having become an image of the true judge who does not judge. When the universe weighs entirely upon us, there is no other possible counterweight than God himself — the true God, for false gods are powerless, even under the name of the true one. Evil is infinite in the sense of the indeterminate: matter, space, time. Over this kind of infinite, only the true infinite prevails. That is why the cross is a balance in which a frail and light body, but which was God, lifted the weight of the entire world. "Give me a fulcrum, and I will lift the world." That fulcrum is the cross. There can be no other. It must be the intersection of the world and of what is not the world. The cross is that intersection.

title: The Impossible
content_html:
Human life is impossible. But only affliction makes one feel it. The impossible good: "Good brings about evil, evil brings about good, and when will it end?" The good is impossible. — But man always has imagination at his disposal to hide from himself this impossibility of the good in each particular case (it is enough, for each event that does not crush us ourselves, to veil a part of the evil and add fictitious good — and some can do this even if they are crushed themselves) and, at the same time, to hide from himself "how much the essence of the necessary differs from that of the good" and to forbid himself from truly encountering God, who is none other than the good itself, which is found nowhere in this world. Desire is impossible; it destroys its object. Lovers cannot be one, nor can Narcissus be two. Don Juan, Narcissus. Because to desire something is impossible, one must desire nothing. Our life is impossibility, absurdity. Each thing we want is contradictory with the conditions or consequences attached to it, each affirmation we make implies the contrary affirmation, all our feelings are mixed with their opposites. This is because we are contradiction, being creatures, being God and infinitely other than God.

Contradiction alone proves that we are not everything. Contradiction is our misery, and the feeling of our misery is the feeling of reality. For our misery, we do not fabricate it. It is true. That is why we must cherish it. All the rest is imaginary.

Impossibility is the door to the supernatural. One can only knock at it. It is another who opens.

One must touch impossibility to escape from the dream. There is no impossibility in dreams. Only powerlessness.

"Our Father, who art in heaven." There is a kind of humor in this. He is your Father, but just try going up to look for him! We are exactly as incapable of detaching ourselves from the ground as an earthworm. And how would he come to us without descending? There is no way of conceiving a relation between God and man that is not as unintelligible as the Incarnation. The Incarnation makes this unintelligibility burst forth. It is the most concrete way of thinking this impossible descent. From that point, why should it not be the truth?

The bonds we cannot tie are the testimony of the transcendent.

We are beings who know, will, and love, and as soon as we bring our attention to bear on the objects of knowledge, will, and love, we recognize with evidence that there are none that are not impossible. Only falsehood can veil this evidence. The consciousness of this impossibility forces us to desire continually to grasp the ungraspable through all that we desire, know, and will.

When something seems impossible to obtain, whatever effort one makes, this indicates an impassable limit at this level and the necessity of a change of level, a breaking through the ceiling. To exhaust oneself in efforts at this level is degrading. It is better to accept the limit, contemplate it, and savor all its bitterness. Error as motive, source of energy. I believe I see a friend. I run to him. A little closer, I realize that the one I am running toward is someone else, a stranger. Likewise, we confuse the relative with the absolute, created things with God. All particular motives are errors. The energy that is supplied by no motive alone is good: obedience to God, that is, insofar as God overflows all that we can imagine or conceive, obedience to nothing. This is at once impossible and necessary — in other words, supernatural. A good deed. It is a good action if, in accomplishing it, one is conscious with one's whole soul that a good deed is something absolutely impossible. To do good. Whatever I do, I know with perfect clarity that it is not the good. For he who is not good does not do good. And "God alone is good"... In every situation, whatever one does, one does evil, and an intolerable evil. One must ask that all the evil one does fall only and directly upon oneself. That is the cross. Good is the action one can accomplish while keeping attention and intention totally oriented toward the pure and impossible good, without veiling by any falsehood either the attraction or the impossibility of the pure good. In this, virtue is entirely analogous to artistic inspiration. Beautiful is the poem one composes while keeping attention oriented toward the inexpressible inspiration, insofar as it is inexpressible.

Contradiction alone proves that we are not everything. Contradiction is our misery, and the feeling of our misery is the feeling of reality. For our misery, we do not fabricate it. It is true. That is why we must cherish it. All the rest is imaginary.

Impossibility is the door to the supernatural. One can only knock at it. It is another who opens.

One must touch impossibility to escape from the dream. There is no impossibility in dreams. Only powerlessness.

"Our Father, who art in heaven." There is a kind of humor in this. He is your Father, but just try going up to look for him! We are exactly as incapable of detaching ourselves from the ground as an earthworm. And how would he come to us without descending? There is no way of conceiving a relation between God and man that is not as unintelligible as the Incarnation. The Incarnation makes this unintelligibility burst forth. It is the most concrete way of thinking this impossible descent. From that point, why should it not be the truth?

The bonds we cannot tie are the testimony of the transcendent.

We are beings who know, will, and love, and as soon as we bring our attention to bear on the objects of knowledge, will, and love, we recognize with evidence that there are none that are not impossible. Only falsehood can veil this evidence. The consciousness of this impossibility forces us to desire continually to grasp the ungraspable through all that we desire, know, and will.

When something seems impossible to obtain, whatever effort one makes, this indicates an impassable limit at this level and the necessity of a change of level, a breaking through the ceiling. To exhaust oneself in efforts at this level is degrading. It is better to accept the limit, contemplate it, and savor all its bitterness. Error as motive, source of energy. I believe I see a friend. I run to him. A little closer, I realize that the one I am running toward is someone else, a stranger. Likewise, we confuse the relative with the absolute, created things with God. All particular motives are errors. The energy that is supplied by no motive alone is good: obedience to God, that is, insofar as God overflows all that we can imagine or conceive, obedience to nothing. This is at once impossible and necessary — in other words, supernatural. A good deed. It is a good action if, in accomplishing it, one is conscious with one's whole soul that a good deed is something absolutely impossible. To do good. Whatever I do, I know with perfect clarity that it is not the good. For he who is not good does not do good. And "God alone is good"... In every situation, whatever one does, one does evil, and an intolerable evil. One must ask that all the evil one does fall only and directly upon oneself. That is the cross. Good is the action one can accomplish while keeping attention and intention totally oriented toward the pure and impossible good, without veiling by any falsehood either the attraction or the impossibility of the pure good. In this, virtue is entirely analogous to artistic inspiration. Beautiful is the poem one composes while keeping attention oriented toward the inexpressible inspiration, insofar as it is inexpressible.
