title: Contradiction
content_html:
The contradictions the mind comes up against are the only realities, the criterion of the real. There is no contradiction in the imaginary. Contradiction is the test of necessity. Contradiction experienced to the depths of one's being is tearing apart, is the cross. When attention fixed on something has made the contradiction within it manifest, a kind of detachment occurs. By persevering along this path, one arrives at detachment. The representable correlation of contraries is an image of the transcendent correlation of contradictories. Every genuine good involves contradictory conditions and is therefore impossible. Whoever keeps attention truly fixed on this impossibility and acts will do good. Likewise, every truth contains a contradiction. Contradiction is the tip of the pyramid. The word good does not have the same meaning as a term in the correlation good-evil and as designating the very being of God. Existence of contrary virtues in the souls of saints. The metaphor of elevation corresponds to this. If I walk along the side of a mountain, I can see first a lake, then, after a few steps, a forest. I must choose: either the lake or the forest. If I want to see both the lake and the forest at once, I must climb higher.

Only the mountain does not exist. It is made of air. One cannot climb: one must be pulled.

Experimental ontological proof. I have in myself no principle of ascent. I cannot climb through the air to heaven. It is only by directing my thought toward something better than myself that this something pulls me upward. If I am truly pulled, that something is real. No imaginary perfection can pull me upward, even by a millimeter. For an imaginary perfection is automatically at the level of the self that imagines it, neither higher nor lower.

This effect of the direction of thought has nothing in common with suggestion. If I tell myself every morning: I am courageous, I am not afraid, I may become courageous, but with a courage that will conform to what, in my present imperfection, I understand by that name and which, consequently, will not go beyond that imperfection. It will be a modification on the same plane, not a change of plane.

Contradiction is the criterion. One cannot procure incompatible things for oneself through suggestion. Only grace can do this. A tender person who becomes courageous through suggestion hardens, often even amputates their own tenderness with a kind of savage pleasure. Only grace can give courage while leaving tenderness intact, or tenderness while leaving courage intact.

The great sorrow of human life, which begins in childhood and continues until death, is that looking and eating are two different operations. Eternal beatitude is a state where looking is eating.

What one looks at here below is not real; it is a stage set. What one eats is destroyed, is no longer real. Sin has produced this separation in us. Natural virtues, if one takes the word virtue in its authentic sense, that is, excluding the social imitations of virtue, are possible as permanent dispositions only for the one who possesses supernatural grace within. Their duration is supernatural. Contraries and contradictories. What the relation of contraries can do to touch the natural being, contradictories thought together can do to touch God. A person inspired by God is one whose behaviors, thoughts, and feelings are linked by a bond that cannot be represented. Pythagorean idea: good is always defined by the union of contraries. When one advocates the opposite of an evil, one remains at the level of that evil. When one has experienced it, one returns to the first. This is what the Gita calls "the bewilderment of opposites." Marxist dialectics is a very degraded and entirely falsified view of this. Bad union of contraries. Worker imperialism developed by Marxism. Latin proverbs on the insolence of newly freed slaves. Insolence and servility aggravate each other. The sincere anarchists, glimpsing through a fog the principle of the union of contraries, believed that by giving power to the oppressed one destroys evil. An impossible dream. What then is specific to the bad and the good union of contraries?

The bad union of contraries (bad because mendacious) is the one that takes place on the plane where the contraries exist. Thus, granting domination to the oppressed: one does not leave the couple oppression-domination.

The good union of contraries takes place on the plane above. Thus, the opposition between domination and oppression is resolved at the level of law, which is equilibrium.

Likewise, pain (and this is its proper function) separates contraries that were united in order to reunite them on the plane above that of their original union. Pulsation of pain-joy. But joy always prevails mathematically.

Pain is violence; joy is gentleness; but joy is the stronger.

The union of contradictories is a tearing apart: it is impossible without extreme suffering.

The correlation of contradictories is detachment. An attachment to a particular thing can only be destroyed by an incompatible attachment. That is why: "Love your enemies... He who does not hate his father and his mother..."

Either one has mastered the contraries, or one is mastered by the contraries.

Simultaneous existence of incompatibles in the behavior of the soul; a scale that tips both ways at once: this is holiness, the realization of the microcosm, the imitation of the order of the world.

Simultaneous existence of contrary virtues in the soul as pincers for reaching God.

To find and formulate certain laws of the human condition of which many profound observations illuminate particular cases.

Thus: what is entirely superior reproduces what is entirely inferior, but transposed.

Kinship of evil with force, with being, and of good with weakness, nothingness.

And at the same time, evil is privation. To elucidate the way contradictories are true.

Method of investigation: as soon as one has thought something, seek in what sense the contrary is true.

Evil is the shadow of good. Every real good, provided with solidity and thickness, casts evil. Only imaginary good casts none.

Since every good is attached to an evil, if one desires good and does not want to spread the corresponding evil around oneself, one is obliged, since one cannot avoid this evil, to concentrate it upon oneself.

Thus the desire for entirely pure good implies the acceptance for oneself, to the utmost degree, of affliction.

If one desires only good, one is in opposition to the law that binds real good to evil as an illuminated object to its shadow; being in opposition to the universal law of the world, it is inevitable that one falls into affliction.

The mystery of the cross of Christ resides in a contradiction, for it is at once a willing offering and a punishment he suffered very much against his will. If one saw in it only the offering, one could wish as much for oneself. But one cannot wish for a punishment suffered against one's will.

title: The Distance Between the Necessary and the Good
content_html:
Necessity is the veil of God. God has entrusted all phenomena without exception to the mechanism of the world. As there is in God the analogue of all human virtues, so also of obedience. This is the play he allows necessity in this world. Necessity, the graspable image of the indifference, the impartiality of God. Thus the ordinary notion of miracle is a kind of impiety (a fact that would have no secondary cause, but only a first cause). The distance between the necessary and the good is the very distance between the creature and the creator. The distance between the necessary and the good. To be contemplated endlessly. The great discovery of Greece. The fall of Troy had no doubt taught them this. Every attempt to justify evil by anything other than: it is, is a fault against this truth. We aspire only to cast off the intolerable burden of the couple good-evil, the burden assumed by Adam and Eve. For this, one must either confuse "the essence of the necessary and that of the good" or leave this world.

To purify evil, there is only God or the social beast. Purity purifies evil. Force also, quite differently. To whoever can do everything, everything is permitted. Whoever serves an omnipotent being can do everything through him. Force delivers from the couple of contraries good-evil. It delivers the one who wields it, and even the one who suffers it. A master has complete license; a slave also. The sword, at the hilt and at the point, delivers from the obligation that is the intolerable weight. Grace also delivers from it, but one reaches grace only through obligation. One escapes the limit only by ascending toward unity or descending toward the unlimited. The limit is the testimony that God loves us. The expectation of the imminent end of the world shaped the behavior of the primitive Church. This belief produced in them "the forgetting of the immense distance that separates the necessary from the good." The absence of God is the most marvelous testimony of perfect love, and this is why pure necessity, necessity manifestly different from good, is so beautiful. The unlimited is the test of the one. Time, of the eternal. The possible, of the necessary. Variation, of the invariant. The value of a science, a work of art, a morality, or a soul is measured by its degree of resistance to this test.

title: Chance
content_html: The beings I love are creatures. They were born by chance. My meeting with them was also chance. They will die. What they think, what they feel, and what they do is limited and mixed with good and evil. To know all this with one's whole soul and to love them no less. To imitate God who infinitely loves finite things as finite things. We wish that everything of value were eternal. But everything of value is the product of an encounter, endures through encounter, and ceases when what had met separates. This is the central thought of Buddhism (a Heraclitean thought). It leads straight to God. Meditation on the chance that brought my father and my mother together is even more salutary than meditation on death. Is there a single thing in me that does not have its origin in that meeting? Only God. And even my thought of God has its origin in that meeting. Stars and fruit trees in blossom. Complete permanence and extreme fragility equally give the feeling of eternity. Theories of progress, of "genius that always breaks through," arise from the fact that it is intolerable to imagine what is most precious in the world delivered over to chance. It is because this is intolerable that it must be contemplated. Creation is precisely this. The only good not subject to chance is the one that lies outside the world. The vulnerability of precious things is beautiful because vulnerability is a mark of existence. Destruction of Troy. Falling petals of fruit trees in blossom. To know that what is most precious is not rooted in existence. This is beautiful. Why? It casts the soul out of time. The woman who wishes for a child white as snow, red as blood, obtains him, but she dies and the child is delivered to a stepmother.

title: He Whom We Must Love Is Absent
content_html:
God can be present in creation only in the form of absence. The evil and the innocence of God. One must place God at an infinite distance in order to conceive him as innocent of evil; reciprocally, evil indicates that God must be placed at an infinite distance. This world, insofar as it is entirely empty of God, is God himself. Necessity, insofar as it is absolutely other than the good, is the good itself. This is why all consolation in affliction distances one from love and truth. This is the mystery of mysteries. When one touches it, one is safe. "In the deserted East..." One must be in a desert. For he whom we must love is absent. He who places his life in faith in God can lose his faith. But he who places his life in God himself will never lose it. To place one's life in what one cannot touch at all. This is impossible. It is a death. This is what is required. Nothing that exists is absolutely worthy of love.

One must therefore love what does not exist. But this object of love that does not exist is not a fiction. For our fictions cannot be more worthy of love than we ourselves, who are not worthy. Consent to the good -- not to any graspable, representable good, but unconditional consent to the absolute good. In consenting to what we represent to ourselves as being good, we consent to a mixture of good and evil, and this consent produces good and evil: the proportion of good and evil in us does not change. On the contrary, unconditional consent to the good that we cannot and will never be able to represent to ourselves -- this consent is pure good and produces only good, and it suffices that it endure for the entire soul eventually to become nothing but good. Faith (when it concerns a supernatural interpretation of the natural) is a conjecture by analogy based on supernatural experiences. Thus those who possess the privilege of mystical contemplation, having experienced the mercy of God, suppose that, God being mercy, the created world is a work of mercy. But as for directly observing this mercy in nature, one must make oneself blind, deaf, and pitiless to believe one can. This is why the Jews and the Muslims, who wish to find in nature the proofs of divine mercy, are merciless. And often Christians too. This is why mysticism is the only source of the virtue of humanity. For not to believe that behind the curtain of the world there is infinite mercy, or to believe that this mercy is in front of the curtain -- both of these make one cruel. There are four testimonies of divine mercy here below. The favors of God to beings capable of contemplation (these states exist and form part of their experience as creatures). The radiance of these beings and their compassion, which is divine compassion in them. The beauty of the world. The fourth testimony is the complete absence of mercy here below. Incarnation. God is weak because he is impartial. He sends the rays of the sun and the rain upon the good and the wicked alike. This indifference of the Father and the weakness of Christ correspond to each other. Absence of God. The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed... God changes nothing in anything. Christ was killed, out of anger, because he was only God. If I thought that God sends me pain by an act of his will and for my good, I would believe I was something, and I would neglect the principal use of pain, which is to teach me that I am nothing. One must therefore think nothing of the sort. But one must love God through pain. I must love being nothing. How horrible it would be if I were something. To love my nothingness, to love being nothingness.

To love with the part of the soul that is on the other side of the curtain, for the part of the soul perceptible to consciousness cannot love nothingness; it is horrified by it. If it believes it loves nothingness, what it loves is something other than nothingness. God sends affliction indiscriminately to the wicked and the good, like rain and sunshine. He did not reserve the cross for Christ. He enters into contact with the individual human being as such only through purely spiritual grace, which responds to the gaze turned toward him -- that is, in the exact measure in which the individual ceases to be one. No event is a favor from God; only grace is. Communion is good for the good and bad for the bad. Thus damned souls are in paradise, but for them paradise is hell. The cry of suffering: why? It resounds through the entire Iliad. To explain suffering is to console it; therefore it must not be explained. Hence the eminent value of the suffering of the innocent. It resembles God's acceptance of evil in creation, God who is innocent. The irreducible character of suffering, which makes it so that one cannot help being horrified by it at the moment one endures it, has as its purpose to halt the will, as absurdity halts the intelligence, as absence halts love, so that, having reached the end of human faculties, one stretches out one's arms, stops, looks, and waits. "He laughs at the affliction of the innocent." Silence of God. The noises of this world imitate that silence. They mean nothing.

It is when we need to the very depths of our being a noise that means something, when we cry out for an answer and it is not granted us, that we touch the silence of God. Usually our imagination puts words into noises, as one idly plays at seeing shapes in smoke. But when we are too exhausted, when we no longer have the courage to play, then we need real words. We cry out for them. The cry tears our very entrails. We obtain only silence. After passing through this, some begin to talk to themselves like madmen. Whatever they do after that, one should feel only pity for them. Others, few in number, give their whole heart to the silence.

If it believes it loves nothingness, what it loves is something other than nothingness. God sends affliction indiscriminately to the wicked and the good, like rain and sunshine. He did not reserve the cross for Christ. He enters into contact with the individual human being as such only through purely spiritual grace, which responds to the gaze turned toward him -- that is, in the exact measure in which the individual ceases to be one. No event is a favor from God; only grace is. Communion is good for the good and bad for the bad. Thus damned souls are in paradise, but for them paradise is hell. The cry of suffering: why? It resounds through the entire Iliad. To explain suffering is to console it; therefore it must not be explained. Hence the eminent value of the suffering of the innocent. It resembles God's acceptance of evil in creation, God who is innocent. The irreducible character of suffering, which makes it so that one cannot help being horrified by it at the moment one endures it, has as its purpose to halt the will, as absurdity halts the intelligence, as absence halts love, so that, having reached the end of human faculties, one stretches out one's arms, stops, looks, and waits. "He laughs at the affliction of the innocent." Silence of God. The noises of this world imitate that silence. They mean nothing.

It is when we need to the very depths of our being a noise that means something, when we cry out for an answer and it is not granted us, that we touch the silence of God. Usually our imagination puts words into noises, as one idly plays at seeing shapes in smoke. But when we are too exhausted, when we no longer have the courage to play, then we need real words. We cry out for them. The cry tears our very entrails. We obtain only silence. After passing through this, some begin to talk to themselves like madmen. Whatever they do after that, one should feel only pity for them. Others, few in number, give their whole heart to the silence.

title: Atheism as Purification
content_html:
A case of true contradictories. God exists; God does not exist. Where is the problem? I am quite certain that there is a God, in the sense that I am quite certain my love is not an illusion. I am quite certain there is no God, in the sense that I am quite certain nothing real resembles what I can conceive when I pronounce that name. But that which I cannot conceive is not an illusion.

There are two atheisms, one of which is a purification of the notion of God.

Perhaps everything that is evil has another aspect that is a purification in the course of progress toward good, and a third that is the higher good.

Three aspects that must be carefully distinguished, for to confuse them is a great danger for thought and for the effective conduct of life.

Between two people who have no experience of God, the one who denies him is perhaps the nearer to him.

The false God who resembles the true one in every respect, except that one does not touch him, prevents one forever from reaching the true one.

To believe in a God who resembles the true one in every respect, except that he does not exist, because one has not reached the point where God exists.

The errors of our age are Christianity without the supernatural. Secularism is the cause -- and first of all, humanism. Religion as a source of consolation is an obstacle to true faith: in this sense, atheism is a purification. I must be an atheist with the part of myself that is not made for God. Among those in whom the supernatural part of themselves is not awakened, the atheists are right and the believers are wrong. A man whose entire family has perished under torture, who has himself been tortured at length in a concentration camp. Or an Indian of the sixteenth century who alone escaped the complete extermination of his entire people. Such men, if they had believed in the mercy of God, either believe in it no longer, or conceive of it quite differently than before. I have not undergone such things. But I know they exist: what difference does that make, then? I must strive to have a conception of divine mercy that does not fade, that does not change, whatever fate sends upon me, and that can be communicated to any human being.

title: Attention and Will
content_html:
Not to understand new things, but to arrive, by dint of patience, effort, and method, at understanding the evident truths with one's whole self.

Levels of belief. The most commonplace truth, when it floods the entire soul, is like a revelation.

Try to remedy faults by attention and not by will.

The will has power only over certain movements of certain muscles, associated with the representation of the displacement of nearby objects. I can will to place my hand flat on the table. If inner purity, or inspiration, or truth in thought were necessarily associated with attitudes of this kind, they could be objects of will. Since they are not, we can only implore them. To implore them is to believe that we have a Father in heaven. Or else to cease desiring them? What could be worse? Inner supplication alone is reasonable, for it avoids the stiffening of muscles that have nothing to do with the matter. What is more foolish than to stiffen one's muscles and clench one's jaw over virtue, or poetry, or the solution of a problem? Attention is something quite different.

Pride is just such a stiffening. There is a lack of grace (in both senses of the word) in the proud person. It is the effect of an error.

Attention, at its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer. It presupposes faith and love. Absolutely unmixed attention is prayer. If one turns the intelligence toward the good, it is impossible that little by little the whole soul should not be drawn to it in spite of itself. Extreme attention is what constitutes the creative faculty in the human being, and there is no extreme attention except religious attention. The quantity of creative genius in a given epoch is rigorously proportional to the quantity of extreme attention, and therefore of authentic religion, in that epoch. Bad way of seeking. Attention fastened on a problem. Another phenomenon of horror of the void. One does not want to have wasted one's effort. Relentlessness in the chase. One must not want to find: as in the case of excessive devotion, one becomes dependent on the object of the effort. One needs an external reward that chance sometimes provides and that one is ready to accept at the price of a distortion of truth. It is only effort without desire (not attached to an object) that infallibly contains a reward. To draw back before the object one pursues. Only what is indirect is effective. One accomplishes nothing if one has not first drawn back. By pulling at the bunch of grapes, one brings the berries to the ground. There are efforts that produce the opposite of the sought-after goal (examples: bitter devotees, false asceticism, certain forms of devotion, etc.). Others are always useful, even when they do not succeed. How to distinguish them?

Perhaps: some are accompanied by the (mendacious) denial of inner wretchedness. Others by attention continually concentrated on the distance between what one is and what one loves.

Love instructs gods and men, for no one learns without desiring to learn. Truth is sought not as truth but as good.

Attention is linked to desire. Not to the will, but to desire. Or, more exactly, to consent.

One liberates energy within oneself. But ceaselessly it attaches itself again. How to liberate it all? One must desire that this be done in us. Truly desire it. Simply desire it, not try to accomplish it. For every attempt in this direction is vain and dearly paid for. In such a work, everything I call "I" must be passive. Only attention -- that attention so full that the "I" disappears -- is required of me. To deprive all that I call "I" of the light of attention and transfer it to the inconceivable.

The capacity to dismiss a thought once and for all is the door of eternity. The infinite in an instant.

Regarding temptations, take the example of the very chaste woman who says nothing in reply to the seducer when he speaks to her and pretends not to hear him.

We must be indifferent to good and evil, but, being indifferent -- that is, projecting the light of attention equally upon both -- good prevails by an automatic phenomenon. This is essential grace. And it is the definition, the criterion, of good.

A divine inspiration operates infallibly, irresistibly, if one does not turn one's attention away from it, if one does not refuse it. There is no choice to be made in its favor; it suffices not to refuse to recognize that it is. Attention turned with love toward God (or, to a lesser degree, toward anything authentically beautiful) makes certain things impossible. Such is the non-acting action of prayer in the soul. There are behaviors that would veil this attention if they occurred, and that, reciprocally, this attention makes impossible. Once one has a point of eternity in the soul, one has nothing more to do than preserve it, for it grows of itself, like a seed. One must maintain around it an armed guard, motionless, and nourish it with the contemplation of numbers, of fixed and rigorous relations. One nourishes the invariant within the soul by the contemplation of the invariant within the body. One writes as one gives birth; one cannot help making the supreme effort. But one acts in the same way. I have no reason to fear not making the supreme effort -- on the sole condition that I do not lie to myself and that I pay attention. The poet produces beauty by attention fixed on what is real. So too does the act of love. To know that this person, who is hungry and thirsty, truly exists as much as I do -- that suffices; the rest follows of itself. The authentic and pure values of truth, beauty, and good in the activity of a human being are produced by one and the same act -- a certain application of the fullness of attention to the object.

Teaching should have as its sole aim the preparation of the possibility of such an act, through the exercise of attention. All other advantages of instruction are of no interest. Studies and faith. Prayer being nothing but attention in its pure form, and studies constituting a gymnastic of attention, each school exercise should be a refraction of spiritual life. A method is needed. A certain way of doing a Latin translation, a certain way of doing a geometry problem (and not just any way) constitutes a gymnastic of attention apt to make it more capable of prayer. Method for understanding images, symbols, etc. Not to try to interpret them, but to look at them until light springs forth. In general, the method for exercising the intelligence consists in looking. Application of this method for the discrimination of the real and the illusory. In sense perception, if one is not sure of what one sees, one shifts position while looking, and the real appears. In the inner life, time takes the place of space. With time one is modified, and if, through the modifications, one keeps one's gaze oriented toward the same thing, illusion eventually dissipates and the real appears. The condition is that attention be a gaze and not an attachment. When there is struggle between the will attached to an obligation and an evil desire, there is a wearing down of the energy attached to the good. One must undergo the bite of desire passively, as a suffering in which one experiences one's wretchedness, and maintain attention turned toward the good. There is then an elevation on the scale of energy qualities.

To steal from desires their energy by removing their orientation in time.

Our desires are infinite in their pretensions but limited by the energy from which they proceed. This is why, with the help of grace, one can master them and, by wearing them out, destroy them. Once this is clearly understood, one has virtually conquered them, if one keeps one's attention in contact with this truth.

Video meliora... In these states, it seems that one thinks the good, and one does think it in a sense, but one does not think its possibility.

The void that one grasps in the pincers of contradiction is incontestably the void from above, for one grasps it all the better as one sharpens the natural faculties of intelligence, will, and love. The void from below is the one into which one falls by allowing the natural faculties to atrophy.

The experience of the transcendent: this seems contradictory, and yet the transcendent can only be known through contact, since our faculties cannot fabricate it.

Solitude. In what, then, does its value consist? For one is in the presence of mere matter (even the sky, the stars, the moon, trees in blossom), of things of lesser worth (perhaps) than a human mind. Its value consists in the higher possibility of attention. If one could be attentive to the same degree in the presence of a human being...

We can know only one thing about God: that he is what we are not. Our wretchedness alone is his image. The more we contemplate it, the more we contemplate him. Sin is nothing other than the failure to recognize human wretchedness. It is unconscious wretchedness, and thereby guilty. The history of Christ is the experimental proof that human wretchedness is irreducible, that in the person absolutely without sin it is as great as in the sinner. It is merely illuminated... Knowledge of human wretchedness is difficult for the rich, for the powerful, because they are almost invincibly led to believe they are something. It is equally difficult for the wretched, because they are almost invincibly led to believe that the rich, the powerful, are something. It is not the fault that constitutes mortal sin, but the degree of light in the soul when the fault, whatever it may be, is committed. Purity is the power to contemplate defilement. Extreme purity can contemplate both the pure and the impure; impurity can contemplate neither: the first frightens it, the second absorbs it. It requires a mixture.

title: Training
content_html:
One must accomplish the possible in order to touch the impossible. The correct exercise, in conformity with duty, of the natural faculties of will, love, and knowledge is to spiritual realities exactly what the movement of the body is to the perception of sensible objects. A paralyzed person does not perceive. The accomplishment of strictly human duty belongs to the same order as correctness in the operations of writing, translating, calculating, etc. To neglect this correctness is a lack of respect toward the object. Likewise, to neglect duty. Things related to inspiration alone are nourished by delays. Those related to natural duty, to the will, suffer no delay. Precepts are not given to be practiced; rather, practice is prescribed for the understanding of precepts. They are scales. One does not play Bach without having practiced scales. But neither does one practice scales for their own sake. Training. -- With each involuntary thought of pride one catches in oneself, turn the full gaze of attention for a few moments upon the memory of a humiliation from one's past life, and choose the bitterest, the most intolerable one possible. One must not try to change or erase within oneself desires and aversions, pleasures and pains. One must undergo them passively, like sensations of color, and without granting them any more credit. If my window is red, I cannot, no matter how much I reason with myself day and night for a year, stop seeing my room in pink. But I also know it is necessary, just, and good that I see it thus. At the same time, I grant this color, as information, only a credit limited by the knowledge of its relation to the window. To accept in this way, and in no other, the desires and aversions, pleasures and pains of every kind that arise in me.

On the other hand, since one also has within oneself a principle of violence -- namely, the will -- one must also, within a limited measure but to the full extent of that measure, use this violent principle violently; compel oneself by violence to act as if one did not have such a desire, such an aversion; try to persuade the sensibility by compelling it to obey. It revolts then, and one must undergo this revolt passively, taste it, savor it, accept it as an external thing, like the pink color of the room whose window is red.

Each time one does violence to oneself in this spirit, one advances a little or a great deal, but really, in the operation of training the animal within.

Of course, for this violence against oneself to truly serve as training, it must be only a simple means. When one trains a dog to be a performing dog, one does not whip it for the sake of whipping, but to train it, and to this end one strikes it only when it misses an exercise. If one whips it without method, one ends by rendering it unfit for all training, and this is what bad asceticism produces.

Violence against oneself is permitted only when it proceeds from reason (with a view to executing what one clearly represents to oneself as duty) -- or else when it is imposed by an irresistible impulse of grace (but then the violence does not proceed from oneself). The source of my difficulties is that through exhaustion, through the absence of vital energy, I am below the level of normal activity. And if something seizes me and lifts me up, I am above it. Then it would seem unfortunate to waste this time on ordinary activities. In other moments, I would have to do violence to myself, and I cannot manage to draw it from within me. I could accept the anomaly of behavior that results. But I know, I believe I know, that I must not. It involves sins of omission toward others. And as for me, it imprisons me. What method, then? If you will, you can make me clean. I must practice transforming the feeling of effort into the passive feeling of suffering. Whatever I may think of it, when God sends me suffering I am indeed forced to suffer all there is to suffer. Why not, in the face of duty, do in the same way all there is to do? Mountains, rocks, fall upon us and hide us from the wrath of the lamb.

I deserve this wrath at present. Not to forget that according to Saint John of the Cross, inspirations that turn one from the accomplishment of easy and lowly obligations come from the wrong side. Duty is given us to kill the self. And I let so precious an instrument rust. One must accomplish one's duty at the prescribed moment in order to believe in the reality of the external world. One must believe in the reality of time. Otherwise one dreams. For years I have recognized this defect in myself, recognized its importance, and done nothing to abolish it. What excuse could I find? Has it not grown in me since the age of ten? But however great it is, it is finite. That suffices. If it is so great as to remove from me the possibility of erasing it during this life, and consequently of attaining the state of perfection, this must be accepted like everything that is, with an acceptance accompanied by love. It suffices that I know it is, that it is bad, that it is finite. But to know effectively each of these three things, and all three together, implies the beginning and the uninterrupted continuation of the process of erasure. If this process does not begin to occur, it is a sign that what I am writing here, I do not truly know. The necessary energy resides in me, since I have enough to live. I must tear it from myself, even if I die of it. There is no other perfect criterion of good and evil than uninterrupted inner prayer. Everything that does not interrupt it is permitted; everything that interrupts it is forbidden. It is impossible to do harm to others when one acts in a state of prayer. On condition that it be genuine prayer. But before reaching that point, one must have worn out one's own will against the observance of rules. Hope is the knowledge that the evil one carries within oneself is finite, and that the slightest orientation of the soul toward the good, even if it lasts only an instant, abolishes some of it, and that in the spiritual domain, every good infallibly produces good. Those who do not know this are condemned to the torment of the Danaids. Infallibly, good produces good and evil produces evil in the domain of the purely spiritual. On the contrary, in the domain of the natural (including the psychological), good and evil produce each other reciprocally. Thus one can have security only once one has reached the domain of the spiritual -- precisely the domain where one can procure nothing for oneself, where one awaits everything from elsewhere.

Each time one does violence to oneself in this spirit, one advances a little or a great deal, but really, in the operation of training the animal within.

Of course, for this violence against oneself to truly serve as training, it must be only a simple means. When one trains a dog to be a performing dog, one does not whip it for the sake of whipping, but to train it, and to this end one strikes it only when it misses an exercise. If one whips it without method, one ends by rendering it unfit for all training, and this is what bad asceticism produces.

Violence against oneself is permitted only when it proceeds from reason (with a view to executing what one clearly represents to oneself as duty) -- or else when it is imposed by an irresistible impulse of grace (but then the violence does not proceed from oneself). The source of my difficulties is that through exhaustion, through the absence of vital energy, I am below the level of normal activity. And if something seizes me and lifts me up, I am above it. Then it would seem unfortunate to waste this time on ordinary activities. In other moments, I would have to do violence to myself, and I cannot manage to draw it from within me. I could accept the anomaly of behavior that results. But I know, I believe I know, that I must not. It involves sins of omission toward others. And as for me, it imprisons me. What method, then? If you will, you can make me clean. I must practice transforming the feeling of effort into the passive feeling of suffering. Whatever I may think of it, when God sends me suffering I am indeed forced to suffer all there is to suffer. Why not, in the face of duty, do in the same way all there is to do? Mountains, rocks, fall upon us and hide us from the wrath of the lamb.

I deserve this wrath at present. Not to forget that according to Saint John of the Cross, inspirations that turn one from the accomplishment of easy and lowly obligations come from the wrong side. Duty is given us to kill the self. And I let so precious an instrument rust. One must accomplish one's duty at the prescribed moment in order to believe in the reality of the external world. One must believe in the reality of time. Otherwise one dreams. For years I have recognized this defect in myself, recognized its importance, and done nothing to abolish it. What excuse could I find? Has it not grown in me since the age of ten? But however great it is, it is finite. That suffices. If it is so great as to remove from me the possibility of erasing it during this life, and consequently of attaining the state of perfection, this must be accepted like everything that is, with an acceptance accompanied by love. It suffices that I know it is, that it is bad, that it is finite. But to know effectively each of these three things, and all three together, implies the beginning and the uninterrupted continuation of the process of erasure. If this process does not begin to occur, it is a sign that what I am writing here, I do not truly know. The necessary energy resides in me, since I have enough to live. I must tear it from myself, even if I die of it. There is no other perfect criterion of good and evil than uninterrupted inner prayer. Everything that does not interrupt it is permitted; everything that interrupts it is forbidden. It is impossible to do harm to others when one acts in a state of prayer. On condition that it be genuine prayer. But before reaching that point, one must have worn out one's own will against the observance of rules. Hope is the knowledge that the evil one carries within oneself is finite, and that the slightest orientation of the soul toward the good, even if it lasts only an instant, abolishes some of it, and that in the spiritual domain, every good infallibly produces good. Those who do not know this are condemned to the torment of the Danaids. Infallibly, good produces good and evil produces evil in the domain of the purely spiritual. On the contrary, in the domain of the natural (including the psychological), good and evil produce each other reciprocally. Thus one can have security only once one has reached the domain of the spiritual -- precisely the domain where one can procure nothing for oneself, where one awaits everything from elsewhere.

title: Intelligence and Grace
content_html:
We know by means of the intelligence that what the intelligence does not apprehend is more real than what it does apprehend. Faith is the experience that the intelligence is illuminated by love. But the intelligence must recognize, by the means proper to it -- that is, by observation and demonstration -- the preeminence of love. It must submit only in knowing why, and in a perfectly precise and clear manner. Otherwise its submission is an error, and what it submits to, despite the label, is something other than supernatural love. It is, for example, social influence. In the domain of the intelligence, the virtue of humility is nothing other than the power of attention. False humility leads one to believe one is nothing insofar as one is oneself, insofar as one is a particular human being. True humility is the knowledge that one is nothing insofar as one is a human being and, more generally, insofar as one is a creature. Intelligence plays a large part in this. One must conceive the universal. When one listens to Bach or a Gregorian melody, all the faculties of the soul are strained and silent, in order to apprehend this perfectly beautiful thing, each in its own way. The intelligence among others: it finds nothing there to affirm or deny, but it is nourished by it. Should not faith be an adhesion of this kind? One degrades the mysteries of faith by making them an object of affirmation or denial, when they should be an object of contemplation. The privileged role of the intelligence in true love comes from the fact that the nature of intelligence consists in being something that effaces itself by the very fact of exercising itself. I can make an effort to reach truths, but when they are there, they are, and I am nothing in the matter. There is nothing closer to true humility than the intelligence. It is impossible to be proud of one's intelligence at the moment one is really exercising it. And when one exercises it, one is not attached to it. For one knows that, were one to become an idiot the very next instant and for the rest of one's life, truth would continue to be. The mysteries of the Catholic faith are not made to be believed by all parts of the soul. The presence of Christ in the host is not a fact in the manner of the presence of Paul's soul in Paul's body (both are completely incomprehensible, but not in the same way). The Eucharist must not therefore be an object of belief for the part of myself that apprehends facts. Here lies the share of truth in Protestantism. But this presence of Christ in the Host is not a symbol, for a symbol is the combination of an abstraction and an image; it is something representable by the human intelligence; it is not supernatural. In this the Catholics are right, not the Protestants. Only the part of oneself that is made for the supernatural should adhere to these mysteries.

The share of the intelligence -- of the part of us that affirms and denies, that forms opinions -- is only submission. Everything I conceive as true is less true than those things whose truth I cannot conceive but which I love. Saint John of the Cross calls faith a night. Among those who have had a Christian upbringing, the lower parts of the soul attach themselves to these mysteries, though they have no right to them. This is why they need a purification whose stages Saint John of the Cross describes. Atheism and unbelief constitute an equivalent of this purification.

The desire to discover something new prevents one from fixing one's thought on the transcendent, unrepresentable meaning of what has already been discovered. My complete lack of talent, which forbids this desire, is a great favor I have received. The recognized and accepted absence of intellectual gifts compels the disinterested exercise of the intelligence.

The object of inquiry must not be the supernatural, but the world. The supernatural is the light: if one makes it an object, one debases it.

The world is a text with several meanings, and one passes from one meaning to another by a labor. A labor in which the body always plays a part, as when one learns the alphabet of a foreign language: this alphabet must enter into the hand by dint of tracing the letters. Apart from this, every change in one's manner of thinking is illusory.

One does not have to choose among opinions: one must welcome them all, but arrange them vertically and place them at the appropriate levels. Thus chance, fate, Providence. The intelligence can never penetrate the mystery, but it can, and it alone can, give an account of the fitness of the words that express it. For this use, it must be sharper, more penetrating, more precise, more rigorous, and more exacting than for any other. The Greeks believed that truth alone befits divine things, not error or approximation, and the divine character of something made them more exacting with regard to exactitude. (We do exactly the opposite, deformed as we are by the habit of propaganda.) It was because they saw in geometry a divine revelation that they invented rigorous demonstration... One must, in the domain of relations between the human being and the supernatural, seek a precision more than mathematical; it must be more precise than science. The rational in the Cartesian sense -- that is, mechanism, humanly representable necessity -- must be assumed wherever possible, in order to bring to light what is irreducible to it. The use of reason makes things transparent to the mind. But one does not see the transparent. One sees the opaque through the transparent, the opaque that was hidden when the transparent was not transparent. One sees either the dust on the window or the landscape behind the window, but never the window itself. Cleaning the dust serves only to see the landscape. Reason must exercise its function only in order to arrive at the true mysteries, the true indemonstrables, which are the real. The not-understood conceals the incomprehensible, and for this reason must be eliminated. Science, today, will seek a source of inspiration above itself or will perish. Science presents only three interests: 1) technical applications; 2) a game of chess; 3) a path toward God. (The game of chess is embellished by competitions, prizes, and medals.) Pythagoras. Only this mystical conception of geometry could furnish the degree of attention necessary for the beginnings of that science. Is it not recognized, moreover, that astronomy emerged from astrology, chemistry from alchemy? But this filiation is interpreted as progress, when in fact there has been a degradation of attention. Transcendent astrology and alchemy are the contemplation of eternal truths in the symbols furnished by the stars and by combinations of substances. Astronomy and chemistry are degradations of these. Astrology and alchemy as magic are even lower degradations. There is fullness of attention only in religious attention. Galileo. Having as its principle unlimited straight-line motion, and no longer circular motion, modern science could no longer be a bridge to God. The philosophical cleansing of the Catholic religion has never been done. To do it, one would have to be both inside and outside.

title: Readings
content_html:
The other. To perceive each human being (image of oneself) as a prison in which a prisoner dwells, with the whole universe around.

Electra, daughter of a powerful father, reduced to slavery, having no hope but in her brother, sees a young man who announces the death of that brother -- and at the most complete moment of despair, it is revealed that this young man is her brother. "They thought it was the gardener." To recognize one's brother in a stranger, to recognize God in the universe.

Justice. To be continually ready to admit that another person is something quite different from what we read when that person is before us (or when we think of that person). Or rather, to read in that person that he or she is certainly something different, perhaps altogether different, from what we read there.

Every being cries out in silence to be read differently.

One reads, but one is also read by others. Interference of these readings. To force someone to read himself as we read him (slavery). To force others to read you as you read yourself (conquest). Mechanism. Most often, a dialogue of the deaf.

Charity and injustice are defined only by readings -- and thus escape all definition. The miracle of the good thief was not that he thought of God, but that he recognized God in his neighbor. Peter before the cock crowed no longer recognized God in Christ.

Others get themselves killed for false prophets, or they read God where he is not. Who can boast of reading rightly? One can be unjust through the will to offend justice, or through a bad reading of justice. But it is almost always the second case. What love of justice guarantees against a bad reading? What is the difference between the just and the unjust if both always act in conformity with the justice they read? Joan of Arc: those who declaim about her today would almost all have condemned her. But her judges did not condemn the saint, the virgin, etc., but the witch, the heretic, etc. The cause of bad readings: public opinion, passions. Public opinion is a very powerful cause. One reads in the story of Joan of Arc what contemporary public opinion dictates. But it was uncertain. And Christ... In fictional moral problems, slander is absent. What hope has innocence if it is not recognized? Readings. Reading -- apart from a certain quality of attention -- obeys gravity. One reads the opinions suggested by gravity (the preponderant share of passions and social conformism in the judgments we make about people and events). With a higher quality of attention, one reads gravity itself, and various possible systems of equilibrium. Superimposed readings: to read necessity behind sensation, to read order behind necessity, to read God behind order. "Judge not." Christ himself does not judge. He is the judgment. Innocent suffering as measure. Judgment, perspective. In this sense every judgment judges the one who makes it. Not to judge. This is not indifference or abstention; it is transcendent judgment, the imitation of divine judgment, which is not possible for us.

title: The Ring of Gyges
content_html:
Other civilizations. Their defects are given as proof of the insufficiency of the religions to which they are attached. Yet in Europe, in the course of the last twenty centuries of history, one could easily find defects at least as great. The destruction of America by massacre and of Africa by slavery, the massacres in the south of France -- these are surely as bad as homosexuality in Greece or orgiastic rites in the East. But it is said that in Europe these defects existed in spite of the perfection of Christianity, and in other civilizations because of the imperfection of their religion. A privileged example, to be contemplated at length, of the mechanism of error. Setting apart. In evaluating India or Greece, one relates the evil to the good. In evaluating Christianity, one sets the evil apart. One sets apart without knowing it -- therein lies the danger. Or, what is worse still, one sets apart by an act of will, but an act of will that is furtive with regard to oneself. And then one no longer knows that one has set apart. One does not want to know it, and by dint of not wanting to know it, one reaches the point of being unable to know it. This faculty of setting apart permits all crimes. For everything outside the domain where education and training have forged solid connections, it constitutes the key to absolute license. This is what allows such incoherent behavior in people, especially whenever the social intervenes -- collective feelings (war, hatred of nations and classes, the patriotism of a party, of a Church, etc.). Everything covered by the prestige of the social is placed in another location from the rest and withdrawn from certain relationships.

One also uses this key when one yields to the attraction of pleasure.

I use it when I put off from day to day the accomplishment of an obligation. I separate the obligation from the passage of time.

There is nothing more desirable than to throw this key away. One would have to throw it to the bottom of a well from which it could never be retrieved.

The ring of Gyges, which makes one invisible, is precisely the act of setting apart. Setting apart oneself and the crime one commits. Not establishing the relation between the two.

The act of throwing away the key, of throwing away the ring of Gyges, is the proper effort of the will; it is the painful and blind march out of the cave.

Gyges. I have become king, and the other king has been assassinated. No connection between these two things. That is the ring.

A factory owner. I have such and such costly pleasures, and my workers suffer from poverty. He may have very sincere pity for his workers and not form the connection.

For no connection forms if thought does not produce it. Two and two remain indefinitely two and two if thought does not add them to make four.

We hate those who would bring us to form the connections we do not wish to form. Justice consists in establishing, among analogous things, identical relations between homothetic terms, even when some of these things concern us personally and are for us the object of an attachment. This virtue is situated at the point of contact between the natural and the supernatural. It belongs to the domain of the will and the clear intelligence, and thus to the cave (for our clarity is darkness), but one cannot maintain oneself in it if one does not pass into the light.

title: The Meaning of the Universe
content_html:
We are a part that must imitate the whole. The atman. Let the soul of a man take the entire universe as its body. Let it have with the entire universe the same relationship as that of a collector to his collection, of one of those soldiers who died crying "Long live the Emperor!" to Napoleon. The soul transports itself, outside the body proper, into something else. Let it therefore transport itself into the entire universe.

To identify oneself with the universe itself. Everything less than the universe is subject to suffering.

I may well die, but the universe goes on. This does not console me if I am other than the universe. But if the universe is to my soul as another body, my death ceases to have more importance for me than that of a stranger. Likewise my sufferings.

Let the entire universe be for me, in relation to my body, what a blind man's stick is in relation to his hand. He truly no longer has his sensitivity in his hand, but at the tip of the stick. An apprenticeship is needed for this.

To restrict one's love to the pure subject and to extend it to the entire universe is the same thing.

To change the relationship between oneself and the world as, through apprenticeship, the worker changes the relationship between himself and his tool. Injury: it is the trade entering the body. Let all suffering make the universe enter the body.

Habit, skill: the transport of consciousness into an object other than the body proper.

Let that object be the universe, the seasons, the sun, the stars.

The relationship between the body and the tool changes through apprenticeship. The relationship between the body and the world must be changed.

One does not detach oneself; one changes one's attachment. To attach oneself to everything.

Through each sensation, to feel the universe. What does it matter then whether it is pleasure or pain? If one's hand is clasped by a beloved person, seen again after a long time, what does it matter if the grip is tight and hurts?

A degree of pain at which one loses the world. But afterward, relief comes. And if the paroxysm returns, the relief returns afterward too. That very degree, if one knows it, becomes expectation of relief, and consequently does not break contact with the world.

Two limiting tendencies: to destroy the self for the sake of the universe, or to destroy the universe for the sake of the self.

He who has not learned to become nothing runs the risk of reaching a moment when all things other than himself cease to exist.

External necessity or imperious inner need, like breathing. "Let us become the central breath." Even if a chest pain makes breathing difficult, one breathes; one cannot do otherwise.

To associate the rhythm of the body's life with that of the world, to feel this association constantly and to feel also the perpetual exchange of matter by which the human being is bathed in the world.

What nothing can take from a human being as long as he lives: as movement where the will has purchase, breathing; as perception, space (even in a dungeon, even with eyes and eardrums pierced, as long as one lives, one perceives space).

To attach to these things the thoughts one wishes no circumstance to take away.

To love one's neighbor as oneself does not mean loving all beings equally, for I do not love all modes of my own existence equally. Nor does it mean never making them suffer, for I do not refuse to make myself suffer. But to have with each one the relationship of one way of thinking the universe to another way of thinking the universe, and not to a part of the universe.

Not to accept an event of the world is to desire that the world not be. Now that is in my power concerning myself; if I desire it, I obtain it. I am then an abscess of the world.

Wishes in folklore: desires have this danger, that they are granted.

To desire that the world not be is to desire that I, as I am, be everything.

May the entire universe, from this pebble at my feet to the most distant stars, exist for me at every moment as much as Agnes for Arnolphe or the cashbox for Harpagon. If I will it, the world can belong to me like the treasure to the miser. But it is a treasure that does not grow. This irreducible "I" that is the irreducible ground of my suffering -- to make it universal. What does it matter that there is never joy in me, since there is perpetual perfect joy in God! And likewise for beauty, intelligence, and all things. To desire one's salvation is bad, not because it is selfish (it is not in man's power to be selfish), but because it directs the soul toward a mere particular and contingent possibility, instead of toward the fullness of being, instead of toward the good which is unconditionally. Everything I desire exists, or has existed, or will exist somewhere. For I cannot invent completely. How then can I not be fulfilled? Br. I could not help imagining him alive, imagining his house as a possible place, for me, of his gentle conversations. Then the awareness of the fact of his death made a dreadful desert. Cold of metal. What did it matter to me that there were other people to love? The love I directed toward him, accompanied by interior sketches, by exchanges that could take place only with him, was without an object. Now I no longer imagine him as alive, and his death is no longer intolerable to me. His memory is sweet to me. But there are others, whom I did not know then, whose death would have the same effect on me.

D... is not dead, but the friendship I bore him is dead, accompanied by a similar pain. He is no more than a shadow.

But I cannot imagine the same transformation for X... Y... Z..., who nevertheless did not exist in my awareness so short a time ago.

Just as parents cannot conceive that a child was nothingness three years before, so one cannot conceive that one has not always known the beings one loves.

I love badly, it seems to me: otherwise things would not happen this way for me. My love would not be attached to a few beings. It would be available for everything that deserves to be loved.

"Be perfect as your heavenly father..." Love as the sun gives light. One must draw one's love back to oneself in order to spread it over all things. God alone loves all things and he loves only himself.

To love in God is far more difficult than one thinks.

I can sully the entire universe with my misery and not feel it, or gather it into myself.

To bear the discord between imagination and fact.

"I am suffering." That is better than "this landscape is ugly."

Not to want to change one's own weight in the balance of the world -- the golden scales of Zeus. The whole cow gives milk, although one draws milk only from the udders. In the same way, the world is productive of holiness.
content_text:
We are a part that must imitate the whole. The atman. Let the soul of a man take the entire universe as its body. Let it have with the entire universe the same relationship as that of a collector to his collection, of one of those soldiers who died crying "Long live the Emperor!" to Napoleon. The soul transports itself, outside the body proper, into something else. Let it therefore transport itself into the entire universe.

To identify oneself with the universe itself. Everything less than the universe is subject to suffering.

I may well die, but the universe goes on. This does not console me if I am other than the universe. But if the universe is to my soul as another body, my death ceases to have more importance for me than that of a stranger. Likewise my sufferings.

Let the entire universe be for me, in relation to my body, what a blind man's stick is in relation to his hand. He truly no longer has his sensitivity in his hand, but at the tip of the stick. An apprenticeship is needed for this.

To restrict one's love to the pure subject and to extend it to the entire universe is the same thing.

To change the relationship between oneself and the world as, through apprenticeship, the worker changes the relationship between himself and his tool. Injury: it is the trade entering the body. Let all suffering make the universe enter the body.

Habit, skill: the transport of consciousness into an object other than the body proper.

Let that object be the universe, the seasons, the sun, the stars.

The relationship between the body and the tool changes through apprenticeship. The relationship between the body and the world must be changed.

One does not detach oneself; one changes one's attachment. To attach oneself to everything.

Through each sensation, to feel the universe. What does it matter then whether it is pleasure or pain? If one's hand is clasped by a beloved person, seen again after a long time, what does it matter if the grip is tight and hurts?

A degree of pain at which one loses the world. But afterward, relief comes. And if the paroxysm returns, the relief returns afterward too. That very degree, if one knows it, becomes expectation of relief, and consequently does not break contact with the world.

Two limiting tendencies: to destroy the self for the sake of the universe, or to destroy the universe for the sake of the self.

He who has not learned to become nothing runs the risk of reaching a moment when all things other than himself cease to exist.

External necessity or imperious inner need, like breathing. "Let us become the central breath." Even if a chest pain makes breathing difficult, one breathes; one cannot do otherwise.

To associate the rhythm of the body's life with that of the world, to feel this association constantly and to feel also the perpetual exchange of matter by which the human being is bathed in the world.

What nothing can take from a human being as long as he lives: as movement where the will has purchase, breathing; as perception, space (even in a dungeon, even with eyes and eardrums pierced, as long as one lives, one perceives space).

To attach to these things the thoughts one wishes no circumstance to take away.

To love one's neighbor as oneself does not mean loving all beings equally, for I do not love all modes of my own existence equally. Nor does it mean never making them suffer, for I do not refuse to make myself suffer. title: Metaxu
content_html:
All created things refuse to be ends for me. Such is the extreme mercy of God toward me. And that itself is evil. Evil is the form that the mercy of God takes in this world.

This world is the closed door. It is a barrier. And at the same time, it is the way through.

Two prisoners in neighboring cells who communicate by knocking on the wall. The wall is what separates them, but it is also what allows them to communicate. So it is with us and God. Every separation is a link.

By placing all our desire for good in a thing, we make that thing a condition of our existence. But we do not thereby make it a good. We always want something other than to exist.

Created things have as their essence to be intermediaries. They are intermediaries leading to one another, and this has no end. They are intermediaries leading to God. To experience them as such.

The bridges of the Greeks. We have inherited them. But we no longer know how to use them. We thought they were meant for building houses on. We have erected skyscrapers on them, to which we ceaselessly add more floors. We no longer know that they are bridges, things made to be crossed over, and that by crossing them one goes to God.

Only he who loves God with a supernatural love can regard means solely as means. Power (and money, that master key of power) is the pure means. For that very reason, it is the supreme end for all those who have not understood. This world, the domain of necessity, offers us absolutely nothing but means. Our will is ceaselessly bounced from one means to another like a billiard ball. All desires are contradictory, like the desire for food. I want the one I love to love me. But if he is totally devoted to me, he no longer exists, and I cease to love him. And as long as he is not totally devoted to me, he does not love me enough. Hunger and satiation. Desire is bad and deceitful, yet without desire one would not seek the true absolute, the true unlimited. One must have passed through it. Misery of beings from whom fatigue removes that surplus energy which is the source of desire. Misery also of those whom desire blinds. One must hitch one's desire to the axis of the poles. What is it sacrilege to destroy? Not what is low, for that is of no importance. Not what is high, for even if one wished to, one cannot touch it. The metaxu. The metaxu are the region of good and evil. To deprive no human being of his metaxu, that is to say, of those relative and mixed goods (home, country, traditions, culture, etc.) that warm and nourish the soul and without which, short of sainthood, a human life is not possible.

True earthly goods are metaxu. One can respect those of others only to the extent that one regards those one possesses merely as metaxu, which implies that one is already on the way toward the point where one can do without them. To respect foreign countries, for example, one must make of one's own country not an idol, but a stepping-stone toward God. All faculties playing freely and without mingling, proceeding from a single principle. This is the microcosm, the imitation of the world. Christ according to Saint Thomas. The Just Man of the Republic. When Plato speaks of specialization, he speaks of the specialization of faculties within man and not of the specialization of men; the same holds for hierarchy. The temporal having meaning only through and for the spiritual, but not being mingled with the spiritual. Leading to it through longing, through surpassing. This is the temporal as bridge, as metaxu. This is the Greek and Provencal vocation. The civilization of the Greeks. No worship of force. The temporal was only a bridge. In states of the soul, they did not seek intensity, but purity.

title: Beauty
content_html:
Beauty is the harmony of chance and the good.

The beautiful is the necessary which, while remaining obedient to its own law and to it alone, obeys the good.

Object of science: the beautiful (that is, order, proportion, harmony) insofar as it is suprasensible and necessary.

Object of art: the sensible and contingent beautiful, perceived through the net of chance and evil.

The beautiful in nature: union of sensory impression and the feeling of necessity. It must be so (in the first place), and precisely so it is.

Beauty seduces the flesh in order to obtain permission to pass through to the soul.

The beautiful contains, among other unities of contraries, that of the instantaneous and the eternal.

The beautiful is that which one can contemplate. A statue, a painting that one can look at for hours.

The beautiful is something to which one can pay attention.

Gregorian music. When one sings the same things for hours each day and every day, whatever is even a little below supreme excellence becomes unbearable and is eliminated.

The Greeks looked at their temples. We tolerate the statues in the Luxembourg Gardens because we do not look at them. A painting such that it could be placed in the cell of a prisoner condemned to perpetual solitary confinement, without that being an atrocity -- on the contrary. Immobile theater is the only truly beautiful theater. Shakespeare's tragedies are of the second order, except Lear. Racine's are of the third order, except Phedre. Corneille's are of the Nth order. A work of art has an author, and yet, when it is perfect, it has something essentially anonymous about it. It imitates the anonymity of divine art. Thus the beauty of the world proves a God who is at once personal and impersonal, and neither one nor the other. The beautiful is a carnal attraction that keeps one at a distance and implies a renunciation. Including the most intimate renunciation, that of the imagination. One wants to eat every other object of desire. The beautiful is that which one desires without wanting to eat it. We desire that it should be. To remain still and unite oneself with what one desires and does not approach. One unites oneself with God in this way: one cannot approach him. Distance is the soul of the beautiful. Gazing and waiting -- that is the attitude corresponding to the beautiful. So long as one can conceive, will, wish, the beautiful does not appear. This is why in all beauty there is contradiction, bitterness, irreducible absence.

Poetry: impossible pain and impossible joy. Poignant touch, nostalgia. Such is Provencal and English poetry. A joy which, by dint of being pure and unmixed, hurts. A pain which, by dint of being pure and unmixed, soothes. Beauty: a fruit one looks at without reaching out one's hand. Likewise a misfortune one looks at without drawing back. Double descending movement: to redo through love what gravity does. Is not the double descending movement the key to all art? The descending movement, mirror of grace, is the essence of all music. The rest serves only to frame it. The rising of notes is a purely sensory rising. The descent is at once a sensory descent and a spiritual ascent. Therein lies the paradise that every being desires: that the slope of nature should lead upward toward the good. In everything that arouses in us the pure and authentic feeling of the beautiful, there is truly the presence of God. There is something like an incarnation of God in the world, of which beauty is the mark. The beautiful is the experimental proof that incarnation is possible. From that point on, all first-rate art is essentially religious. (This is what we no longer know today.) A Gregorian melody bears witness as much as the death of a martyr. If the beautiful is the real presence of God in matter, if contact with the beautiful is a sacrament in the full sense of the word, how is it that there are so many perverse aesthetes? Nero. Does this resemble the hunger of devotees of black masses for consecrated hosts? Or, more probably, do these people not attach themselves to authentic beauty, but to a bad imitation? For just as there is a divine art, there is a demonic art. It was no doubt the latter that Nero loved. A large part of our art is demonic. A passionate lover of music may well be a wicked man -- but I would find it hard to believe this of someone who thirsts for Gregorian chant. We must indeed have committed crimes that have made us accursed, since we have lost all the poetry of the universe. Art has no immediate future because all art is collective and there is no longer any collective life (there are only dead collectivities), and also because of this rupture of the true pact between body and soul. Greek art coincided with the beginnings of geometry and with athletics, medieval art with craftsmanship, Renaissance art with the beginnings of mechanics, etc. Since 1914 there has been a complete break. Even comedy is almost impossible; there is room only for satire (when has it been easier to understand Juvenal?). Art can be reborn only from the heart of the great anarchy -- epic no doubt, because misfortune will have simplified many things... It is therefore quite useless on your part to envy da Vinci or Bach. Greatness, in our day, must take other paths. It can, moreover, only be solitary, obscure, and without echo... (yet there is no art without echo).

title: Algebra
content_html:
Money, machinery, algebra. The three monsters of contemporary civilization. Complete analogy. Algebra and money are essentially levelers, the first intellectually, the second effectively. The life of Provencal peasants ceased to resemble that of the Greek peasants described by Hesiod about fifty years ago. Destruction of science as the Greeks conceived it around the same period. Money and algebra triumphed simultaneously. The relationship of sign to signified perishes; the play of exchanges between signs multiplies by itself and for itself. And the growing complication requires signs of signs... Among the characteristics of the modern world, one must not forget the impossibility of thinking concretely about the relationship between effort and the result of effort. Too many intermediaries. As in other cases, this relationship which lies in no thought lies in a thing: money. Since collective thought cannot exist as thought, it passes into things (signs, machines...). Hence this paradox: it is the thing that thinks and man who is reduced to the state of a thing. There is no collective thought. On the other hand, our science is collective like our technology. Specialization. One inherits not only results but also methods one does not understand. Moreover, the two are inseparable, for the results of algebra furnish methods for the other sciences.

To take inventory of or to criticize our civilization -- what does that mean? To seek to clarify precisely the trap that has made man the slave of his own creations. Where has unconsciousness infiltrated into methodical thought and action? Escape into the wild life is a lazy solution. The original pact between mind and world must be recovered within the very civilization in which we live. This is moreover a task impossible to accomplish because of the brevity of life and the impossibility of collaboration and succession. That is no reason not to undertake it. We are all in a situation analogous to that of Socrates when he was awaiting death in his prison and was learning to play the lyre... At least one will have lived...

The mind succumbing under the weight of quantity has no other criterion than efficacy.

Modern life is given over to excess. Excess invades everything: action and thought, public and private life. Hence the decadence of art. There is no longer balance anywhere. The Catholic movement is partially a reaction against this: Catholic ceremonies, at least, have remained intact. But also they are without relation to the rest of existence.

Capitalism has achieved the emancipation of the human collectivity from nature. But this collectivity has assumed, in relation to the individual, the succession of the oppressive function formerly exercised by nature.

This is true even materially. Fire, water, etc. All these forces of nature, the collectivity has seized them. Question: can one transfer to the individual this emancipation won by society?
