title: The Social Letter
content_html:
Man is a slave insofar as between action and its effect, between effort and the finished work, there is placed the intervention of alien wills. This is the case both for the slave and for the master today. Never is man face to face with the conditions of his own activity. Society is a screen between nature and man. To be face to face with nature and not with men is the only discipline. To depend on an alien will is to be a slave. Now that is the lot of all men. The slave depends on the master and the master on the slave. A situation that makes one either suppliant or tyrannical or both at once (omnia serviliter pro dominatione). On the contrary, face to face with inert nature, one has no other resource than to think. The notion of oppression is basically a stupidity -- one has only to read the Iliad. And, a fortiori, the notion of an oppressive class. One can only speak of an oppressive structure of society. Difference between the slave and the citizen (Montesquieu, Rousseau...): the slave is subject to his master and the citizen to the laws. In other respects, the master may be very gentle and the laws very harsh: that changes nothing. Everything lies in the distance between caprice and rule. Why is subordination to caprice slavery? The ultimate cause lies in the relationship between the soul and time. He who is subject to the arbitrary is suspended from the thread of time; he waits (the most humiliating situation...) for what the next instant will bring. He does not dispose of his instants; the present is no longer for him a lever pressing upon the future. To find oneself face to face with things frees the mind. To find oneself face to face with men degrades, if one depends on them, and this whether the dependence takes the form of submission or that of command. Why these men between nature and me? Never to have to reckon with an unknown thought... (for then one is given over to chance). Remedy: outside of fraternal bonds, to treat men as a spectacle and never to seek friendship. To live among men as in that railway car from Saint-Etienne to Le Puy... Above all, never to allow oneself to dream of friendship. Everything is paid for. Rely only on yourself. Beyond a certain degree of oppression, the powerful necessarily come to be adored by their slaves. For the thought of being absolutely constrained, the plaything of another being, is unbearable for a human being. Therefore, if all means of escaping the constraint are taken from him, he has no other resource than to persuade himself that the very things to which he is constrained, he accomplishes voluntarily, in other words, to substitute devotion for obedience. And he will even sometimes strive to do more than is imposed on him, and will suffer less from it, by the same phenomenon by which children endure laughingly, when they are playing, physical pains that would crush them if inflicted as punishment. It is by this detour that servitude degrades the soul: for this devotion rests on a lie, since its reasons do not bear examination. (In this regard, the Catholic principle of obedience must be considered liberating, whereas Protestantism rests on the idea of sacrifice and devotion.) The only salvation consists in replacing the unbearable idea of constraint, no longer with the illusion of devotion, but with the notion of necessity.

On the contrary, revolt, if it does not immediately pass into precise and effective actions, always changes into its opposite, because of the humiliation produced by the feeling of radical impotence that results from it. In other words, the principal support of the oppressor lies precisely in the impotent revolt of the oppressed.

One could write in this vein the novel of a conscript of Napoleon.

And the lie of devotion deceives the master too...

Always consider men in power as dangerous things. Guard against them as far as one can without despising oneself. And if one day one finds oneself compelled, on pain of cowardice, to go and shatter oneself against their power, consider oneself vanquished by the nature of things and not by men. One can be in a dungeon and in chains, but one can also be struck by blindness or paralysis. There is no difference.

The only way to preserve one's dignity in forced submission: to consider the chief as a thing. Every man is a slave to necessity, but the conscious slave is far superior.

Social problem. To restrict to a minimum the amount of the supernatural indispensable for making social life bearable. Everything that tends to increase it is bad (it is tempting God). Misfortune must be eliminated from social life as far as possible, for misfortune serves only grace, and society is not a society of the elect. There will always be enough misfortune for the elect.

title: The Great Beast
content_html:
The great beast is the only object of idolatry, the only ersatz of God, the only imitation of an object that is infinitely distant from me and that is me. If one could be selfish, that would be quite pleasant. It would be rest. But literally one cannot. It is impossible for me to take myself as an end, nor consequently to take my fellow being as an end, since he is my fellow. Nor any material object, for matter is even less capable of receiving finality than human beings. One single thing here below can be taken as an end, for it possesses a kind of transcendence with respect to the human person: the collective. The collective is the object of all idolatry; it is what chains us to the earth. Avarice: gold is social. Ambition -- power is social. Science, art too. And love? Love is more or less an exception; that is why one can go to God through love, but not through avarice or ambition. Yet the social is not absent from love (passions excited by princes, famous people, all those who have prestige...). There are two goods, bearing the same name but radically different -- the good that is the opposite of evil and the good that is the absolute. The absolute has no opposite. The relative is not the opposite of the absolute; it derives from it by a non-commutative relation. What we want is the absolute good. What we can attain is the good correlative to evil. We tend toward it by mistake, like the Prince who prepares to love the servant instead of the mistress. It is the clothing that causes the mistake. It is the social that casts upon the relative the color of the absolute. The remedy lies in the idea of relation. Relation bursts violently out of the social. It is the monopoly of the individual. Society is the cave; the way out is solitude. Relation belongs to the solitary mind. No crowd conceives relation. This is good or evil in regard to... to the extent that... That escapes the crowd. A crowd does not do an addition. He who is above social life re-enters it when he wishes; not he who is below. The same holds for everything. Non-commutative relation between the better and the less good. The vegetative and the social are the two domains where the good does not enter. Christ redeemed the vegetative, not the social. He did not pray for the world. The social is irreducibly the domain of the prince of this world. One has no duty toward the social except to try to limit the evil (Richelieu: the salvation of states is only in this world). A society with divine pretensions like the Church is perhaps more dangerous through the ersatz of good it contains than through the evil that stains it. A divine label on the social: an intoxicating mixture that licenses everything. The devil in disguise. Conscience is deceived by the social. Surplus energy (imaginative) is largely attached to the social. It must be detached from it. This is the most difficult detachment.

Meditation on the social mechanism is in this regard a purification of the first importance.

To contemplate the social is as good a way as withdrawing from the world. That is why I was not wrong to be so long involved with politics.

It is only through entry into the transcendent, the supernatural, the authentically spiritual that man becomes superior to the social. Until then, in fact, whatever he does, the social is transcendent with respect to man.

On the non-supernatural plane, society is what separates from evil (from certain forms of evil) as by a barrier; a society of criminals or the depraved, even if composed of just a few men, removes this barrier.

But what drives one to enter such a society? Either necessity, or frivolity, or, most often, a mixture of both; one does not believe one is committing oneself, for one does not know that, apart from the supernatural, society alone prevents one from naturally passing into the most atrocious forms of vice or crime. One does not know that one is going to become other, for one does not know how far the domain of what is modifiable by the external extends in oneself. One always commits oneself without knowing.

Rome is the great beast that is atheist, materialist, adoring only itself. Israel is the great beast that is religious. Neither one nor the other is lovable. The great beast is always repugnant.

Is a society ruled only by gravity viable, or is a little of the supernatural a vital necessity? In Rome, perhaps, gravity alone. Among the Hebrews perhaps also. Their God was heavy. Perhaps only one ancient people was absolutely without mysticism: Rome. By what mystery? An artificial city made of fugitives, like Israel. Plato's great beast. Marxism, insofar as it is true, is entirely contained in Plato's page on the great beast, and its refutation is contained there too. Force of the social. Agreement among several men contains a sense of reality. It also contains a sense of duty. Deviation from this agreement appears as a sin. Thereby all reversals are possible. A state of conformity is an imitation of grace. By a singular mystery -- which comes from the power of the social -- a profession gives average men, for the objects pertaining to it, virtues which, if they extended to all circumstances of life, would make them heroes or saints. But the power of the social makes these virtues natural. So they need compensation. Pharisees: "Truly I say to you, they have received their reward." Conversely, Christ could say of publicans and prostitutes: truly I say to you, they have received their punishment -- namely, social reprobation. Insofar as they have it, the Father who is in secret does not punish them. Whereas sins not accompanied by social reprobation receive the full measure of punishment from the Father who is in secret. Thus social reprobation is a favor of fortune. But it turns into additional evil for those who, under pressure of this reprobation, fashion for themselves an eccentric social milieu within which they have license. Milieux of criminals, of homosexuals, etc. The service of the false God (of the social Beast in whatever incarnation) purifies evil by eliminating the horror of it. To whoever serves it, nothing seems evil except failures in the service. But the service of the true God leaves intact and even intensifies the horror of evil. This evil that one regards with horror, at the same time one loves as emanating from the will of God. Those who today believe that one of the adversaries is on the side of good also believe that it will have the victory. To look upon a good, loved as such, as condemned by the near course of events is an intolerable pain. The idea that what no longer exists at all could be a good is painful, and one pushes it away. That is submission to the great beast. The fortitude of the communists comes from the fact that they tend not only toward what they believe to be good, but toward what they believe is ineluctably and imminently going to happen. Thus, without being saints -- far from it -- they can endure dangers and sufferings that only a saint would endure for justice alone. In certain respects, the state of mind of the communists is very analogous to that of the early Christians.

This eschatological propaganda explains very well the persecutions of the early period. "He to whom little is forgiven loves little." This concerns the person in whom social virtue occupies a large place. Grace finds little free space in him. Obedience to the great beast in conformity with good -- that is social virtue. A Pharisee is a man who is virtuous by obedience to the great beast. Charity can and must love in all countries everything that is a condition of the spiritual development of individuals, that is to say, on the one hand, social order, even if it is bad, as being less bad than disorder, on the other hand, language, ceremonies, customs, everything that partakes of the beautiful, all the poetry that envelops the life of a country. But a nation as such cannot be an object of supernatural love. It has no soul. It is a great beast. And yet a city... But that is not of the social; it is a human milieu of which one is no more conscious than of the air one breathes. A contact with nature, the past, tradition. Rootedness is something other than the social. Patriotism. One should have no other love than charity. A nation cannot be an object of charity. But a country can be, as a milieu bearing eternal traditions. All countries can be.

title: Israel
content_html:
Christendom became totalitarian, conquering, exterminatory because it did not develop the notion of the absence and non-action of God here below. It clung to Jehovah as much as to Christ; it conceived Providence in the manner of the Old Testament: Israel alone could resist Rome because it resembled it, and nascent Christianity thus bore the Roman stain before becoming the official religion of the Empire. The harm done by Rome was never truly repaired. God made to Moses and Joshua purely temporal promises at a time when Egypt was straining toward the eternal salvation of the soul. The Hebrews, having refused the Egyptian revelation, had the God they deserved: a carnal and collective God who until the exile spoke to the soul of no one (unless, in the Psalms)?... Among the characters of the Old Testament narratives, only Abel, Enoch, Noah, Melchizedek, Job, and Daniel are pure. It is not surprising that a people of fugitive slaves, conquerors of a paradisiacal land prepared by civilizations in whose labor they had had no part and which they destroyed by massacres -- that such a people could not have produced much good. To speak of a "God who educates" in connection with this people is an atrocious joke. There is nothing surprising in the fact that there is so much evil in a civilization -- ours -- vitiated at its base and in its very inspiration by this dreadful lie. The curse of Israel weighs upon Christendom. The atrocities, the Inquisition, the exterminations of heretics and infidels -- that was Israel. Capitalism was Israel, notably among its worst enemies. There can be no personal contact between man and God except through the person of the Mediator. Apart from the Mediator, the presence of God to man can only be collective, national. Israel simultaneously chose the national God and rejected the Mediator; it perhaps tended from time to time toward true monotheism, but always fell back, and could not help falling back, to a tribal God. The man who has contact with the supernatural is essentially a king, for he is the presence in society, in the form of an infinitely small thing, of an order transcendent to the social. But the place he occupies in the social hierarchy is entirely indifferent. As for greatness in the social order, only he who has captured a large part of the energy of the great beast is capable of it. But he cannot have part in the supernatural. Moses, Joshua -- that is the share of the supernatural for those who have captured much social energy. Israel is an attempt at supernatural social life. It succeeded, one may suppose, in the best possible way of the kind. Useless to try again. The result shows of what divine revelation the great beast is capable. Isaiah is the first to bring pure light. Israel resisted Rome because its God, though immaterial, was a temporal sovereign on a level with the Emperor, and it is thanks to this that Christianity could be born. The religion of Israel was not elevated enough to be fragile, and thanks to this solidity it could protect the growth of what is most elevated.

It was necessary that Israel should be ignorant of the idea of the Incarnation in order that the Passion be possible. Rome too (these were perhaps the only two peoples to be ignorant of it). But Israel had to have some part in God. All the part possible without spirituality or the supernatural. An exclusively collective religion. It is through this ignorance, through these shadows that it was the chosen people. Thus one can understand Isaiah's word: "I have hardened their hearts so that they might not hear my word."

It is for this reason that everything is stained with sin in Israel, because there is nothing pure without participation in the incarnate divinity, and so that the lack of such participation would be manifest.

Is not the great stain the struggle of Jacob with the angel: "The Lord... will render justice to Jacob according to his works. From the maternal womb he supplanted his brother, and in his manhood he triumphed over a God. He struggled against an angel and was victorious, and the angel wept and begged for mercy..."

Is it not the great misfortune, when one struggles against God, not to be vanquished?

Israel. Everything is stained and atrocious, as if on purpose, from Abraham onward (except for a few prophets). As if to indicate quite clearly: Warning! here is evil!

A people chosen for blindness, chosen to be the executioner of Christ.

The Jews, this handful of uprooted people, caused the uprooting of the entire globe. Their part in Christianity made Christendom a thing uprooted from its own past. The attempt at re-rooting of the Renaissance failed because it was anti-Christian in orientation. The tendency of the "Enlightenment," 1789, secularism, etc., have infinitely increased the uprooting through the lie of progress. And uprooted Europe uprooted the rest of the world through colonial conquest. Capitalism, totalitarianism are part of this progression in uprooting; the anti-Semites, naturally, propagate the Jewish influence. But before they uprooted by poison, Assyria in the East, Rome in the West had uprooted by the sword.

Primitive Christianity manufactured the poison of the notion of progress through the idea of a divine pedagogy forming men to make them capable of receiving the message of Christ. This agreed with the hope of the universal conversion of nations and the end of the world as imminent phenomena. But since neither of these occurred, after seventeen centuries this notion of progress was prolonged beyond the moment of the Christian Revelation. From that point on, it was bound to turn against Christianity.

The other poisons mixed with the truth of Christianity are of Jewish origin. This one is specifically Christian.

The metaphor of divine pedagogy dissolves individual destiny, which alone counts for salvation, into that of peoples.

Christianity sought to find a harmony in history. This is the germ of Hegel and Marx. The notion of history as directed continuity is Christian.

It seems to me that few ideas are more completely false. To seek harmony in becoming, in what is the contrary of eternity. A bad union of contraries. Humanism and what followed from it is not a return to Antiquity, but a development of poisons internal to Christianity. It is supernatural love that is free. By wanting to force it, one substitutes a natural love for it. But conversely, freedom without supernatural love, the freedom of 1789, is entirely empty, a mere abstraction, without any possibility of ever becoming real.

It succeeded, one may suppose, in the best possible way of the kind. Useless to try again. The result shows of what divine revelation the great beast is capable. Isaiah is the first to bring pure light. Israel resisted Rome because its God, though immaterial, was a temporal sovereign on a level with the Emperor, and it is thanks to this that Christianity could be born. The religion of Israel was not elevated enough to be fragile, and thanks to this solidity it could protect the growth of what is most elevated.

It was necessary that Israel should be ignorant of the idea of the Incarnation in order that the Passion be possible. Rome too (these were perhaps the only two peoples to be ignorant of it). But Israel had to have some part in God. All the part possible without spirituality or the supernatural. An exclusively collective religion. It is through this ignorance, through these shadows that it was the chosen people. Thus one can understand Isaiah's word: "I have hardened their hearts so that they might not hear my word."

It is for this reason that everything is stained with sin in Israel, because there is nothing pure without participation in the incarnate divinity, and so that the lack of such participation would be manifest.

Is not the great stain the struggle of Jacob with the angel: "The Lord... will render justice to Jacob according to his works. From the maternal womb he supplanted his brother, and in his manhood he triumphed over a God. He struggled against an angel and was victorious, and the angel wept and begged for mercy..."

Is it not the great misfortune, when one struggles against God, not to be vanquished?

Israel. Everything is stained and atrocious, as if on purpose, from Abraham onward (except for a few prophets). As if to indicate quite clearly: Warning! here is evil!

A people chosen for blindness, chosen to be the executioner of Christ.

The Jews, this handful of uprooted people, caused the uprooting of the entire globe. Their part in Christianity made Christendom a thing uprooted from its own past. The attempt at re-rooting of the Renaissance failed because it was anti-Christian in orientation. The tendency of the "Enlightenment," 1789, secularism, etc., have infinitely increased the uprooting through the lie of progress. And uprooted Europe uprooted the rest of the world through colonial conquest. Capitalism, totalitarianism are part of this progression in uprooting; the anti-Semites, naturally, propagate the Jewish influence. But before they uprooted by poison, Assyria in the East, Rome in the West had uprooted by the sword.

Primitive Christianity manufactured the poison of the notion of progress through the idea of a divine pedagogy forming men to make them capable of receiving the message of Christ. This agreed with the hope of the universal conversion of nations and the end of the world as imminent phenomena. But since neither of these occurred, after seventeen centuries this notion of progress was prolonged beyond the moment of the Christian Revelation. From that point on, it was bound to turn against Christianity.

The other poisons mixed with the truth of Christianity are of Jewish origin. This one is specifically Christian.

The metaphor of divine pedagogy dissolves individual destiny, which alone counts for salvation, into that of peoples.

Christianity sought to find a harmony in history. This is the germ of Hegel and Marx. The notion of history as directed continuity is Christian.

It seems to me that few ideas are more completely false. To seek harmony in becoming, in what is the contrary of eternity. A bad union of contraries. Humanism and what followed from it is not a return to Antiquity, but a development of poisons internal to Christianity. It is supernatural love that is free. By wanting to force it, one substitutes a natural love for it. But conversely, freedom without supernatural love, the freedom of 1789, is entirely empty, a mere abstraction, without any possibility of ever becoming real.

title: Social Harmony
content_html:
With respect to any given order, a superior order, hence infinitely above it, can be represented in the first only by an infinitely small thing. The mustard seed, the instant as image of eternity, etc.

Point of contact between the circle and the straight line (tangent). This is the presence of the superior order in the inferior order in the form of an infinitely small thing.

Christ is the point of tangency between humanity and God.

The discretion, the infinitesimal character of pure good...

Equilibrium is the submission of one order to another, an order transcendent to the first and present in the first in the form of an infinitely small thing.

Thus a true kingship would be the perfect city.

Each person, in society, is the infinitely small thing that represents the order transcendent to the social and infinitely greater.

The love of citizen for city, of vassal for lord, should be supernatural love.

Equilibrium alone destroys, annuls force. The social order can only be an equilibrium of forces.

Since one cannot expect a man without grace to be just, a society must be organized in such a way that injustices punish one another in a perpetual oscillation. Equilibrium alone annihilates force. If one knows where society is off balance, one must do what one can to add weight to the lighter side. Although the weight is evil, in handling it with this intention, perhaps one does not defile oneself. But one must have conceived equilibrium and be always ready to change sides, like justice, "that fugitive from the camp of the victors." Meaning of the famous passage in the Gorgias on geometry. No unlimited development is possible in the nature of things; the world rests entirely on measure and balance, and it is the same in the city. All ambition is excess, absurdity. geometrias gar ameleis. What the ambitious man totally forgets is the notion of proportion.

Stupid people to whom my power chains me, alas! my very pride has need of your arms.

The feudal bond, by making obedience a thing from man to man, greatly diminishes the share of the great beast. Better still, the law. One should obey only the law or a man. This is almost the case with monastic orders. The city should be built on this model.

To obey the lord, a man, but naked, adorned only with the majesty of the oath, and not with a majesty borrowed from the great beast. A well-made society would be one in which the state had only a negative action, of the order of a rudder: a slight pressure at the opportune moment to compensate for a beginning of imbalance. The meaning of Plato's Statesman is that power must be exercised by a social milieu composed of victors and vanquished. But this is against nature, except when the victors are barbarians. In this regard, the victory of barbarians over the civilized, when it is not destructive, is more fruitful than that of the civilized over the barbarians. Technology, which places force and civilization on the same side, makes these regenerations impossible. It is accursed. Outside of these moments of intermixing, to share force between the strong and the weak is possible only with the intervention of a supernatural factor. What is supernatural in society is legitimacy in its double form: law and attribution of the highest power. A monarchy tempered by laws could perhaps effect the mixture of the Statesman. But there can be no legitimacy without religion. Obedience to a man whose authority is not illuminated by legitimacy is a nightmare. The only thing that can make of pure legitimacy, an idea absolutely devoid of force, something sovereign, is the thought: this has always been, this will always be.

That is why a reform must always appear either as a return to a past that had been allowed to deteriorate, or as an adaptation of an institution to new conditions, an adaptation whose aim is not change, but on the contrary the maintenance of an invariant relation, as if one has the ratio 12/4 and 4 becomes 5, the true conservative is not the one who wants 12/5, but the one who makes 12 into 15. The existence of a legitimate authority places finality in the labors and acts of social life, a finality other than the thirst to grow (the sole motive recognized by liberalism). Legitimacy is continuity in time, permanence, an invariant. It gives as finality to social life something that exists and is conceived as having always been and as bound always to be. It obliges men to will exactly what is. The rupture of legitimacy, uprooting when it is not due to conquest, when it occurs in a country as a result of the abuse of legitimate authority, inevitably gives rise to the obsessive idea of progress, for finality then turns toward the future. Atheistic materialism is necessarily revolutionary, for in order to orient oneself toward an absolute good of this world, one must place it in the future. One then needs, for this impulse to be complete, a mediator between future perfection and the present. This mediator is the leader: Lenin, etc. He is infallible and perfectly pure. Through him, evil becomes good. One must either be like this, or love God, or let oneself be tossed about by the small evils and small goods of daily life.

The link between progress and the base level (because what one generation can pursue from the point where the preceding one stopped is necessarily external) is an example of the kinship between force and baseness. The great error of the Marxists and of the entire nineteenth century was to believe that by walking straight ahead one had risen into the air. The atheistic idea par excellence is the idea of progress, which is the negation of the experimental ontological proof, for it implies that the mediocre can of itself produce the better. Now all modern science converges toward the destruction of the idea of progress. Darwin destroyed the illusion of internal progress that was in Lamarck. The theory of mutations leaves only chance and elimination. Thermodynamics posits that energy degrades and never rises, and this applies even to plant and animal life. Psychology and sociology will be scientific only through an analogous use of the notion of energy, a use incompatible with any idea of progress, and then they will shine with the light of true faith. The eternal alone is invulnerable to time. For a work of art to be admired forever, for a love, a friendship to last a whole life (even to last pure for a whole day perhaps), for a conception of the human condition to remain the same through the multiple experiences and vicissitudes of fortune -- an inspiration is needed that descends from the other side of the sky. A wholly impossible future, like the ideal of the Spanish anarchists, degrades far less, differs far less from the eternal than a possible future. It does not degrade at all, except through the illusion of possibility. If it is conceived as impossible, it transports into the eternal. The possible is the place of imagination, and therefore of degradation. One must will either what precisely exists or what cannot exist at all, better still both. What is and what cannot be are both outside of becoming. The past, when the imagination does not indulge in it -- at the moment when some encounter makes it surge forth in its purity -- is time with the color of eternity. The feeling of reality there is pure. That is pure joy. That is the beautiful. Proust. The present, we are attached to it. The future, we fabricate it in our imagination. Only the past, when we do not refabricate it, is pure reality. Time, in its course, wears away and destroys what is temporal. That is why there is more eternity in the past than in the present. Value of rightly understood history, analogous to that of memory in Proust. Thus the past presents us with something that is at once real and better than we, and that can draw us upward, which the future never does. Past: the real, but absolutely beyond our reach, toward which we cannot take a step, toward which we can only orient ourselves so that an emanation of it may come to us. In this, it is the image par excellence of eternal, supernatural reality. Is it for this reason that there is joy and beauty in memory as such? Whence shall our renewal come, for us who have sullied and emptied the entire globe? From the past alone, if we love it.

The contraries. Today there is both thirst and disgust for totalitarianism, and almost everyone loves one totalitarianism and hates another. Is there always identity between what one loves and what one hates? What one hates, does one always feel the need to love in another form, and conversely? The constant illusion of Revolution consists in believing that since the victims of force, being innocent of the violence taking place, if one puts force in their hands, they will use it justly. But except for souls close enough to sainthood, the victims are defiled by force as much as the executioners. The evil at the hilt of the sword is transmitted to the point. And the victims, thus placed at the summit and intoxicated by the change, do as much harm or more, then soon fall back again. Socialism consists in placing the good in the vanquished, and racism in the victors. But the revolutionary wing of socialism makes use of those who, though born below, are by nature and vocation victors, and so it arrives at the same ethic. Modern totalitarianism is to the Catholic totalitarianism of the twelfth century what the secular and Masonic spirit is to the humanism of the Renaissance. Humanity degrades at each oscillation. How far will this go? After the collapse of our civilization, one of two things: either it will perish entirely, as the ancient civilizations did, or it will adapt to a decentralized world. It depends on us, not to break the centralization (for it automatically snowballs until catastrophe), but to prepare the future.

Our epoch has destroyed the inner hierarchy. How could it leave the social hierarchy standing, which is only a crude image of it? You could not have been born at a better time than this, when everything has been lost.

title: The Mysticism of Work
content_html:
The secret of the human condition is that there is no equilibrium between man and the surrounding forces of nature that infinitely surpass him in inaction; there is equilibrium only in action, by which man recreates his own life through work. The greatness of man is always to recreate his life. To recreate what is given to him. To forge the very thing he undergoes. Through work, he produces his own natural existence. Through science, he recreates the universe by means of symbols. Through art, he recreates the alliance between his body and his soul (cf. the discourse of Eupalinos). Note that each of these three things is something poor, empty, and vain, taken in itself and apart from its relation to the other two. Union of the three: working-class culture (you can always wait for that)... Plato himself is only a precursor. The Greeks knew art and sport, but not work. The master is the slave of the slave in the sense that the slave produces the master. Two tasks: to individualize the machine. To individualize science (popularization, a people's university in Socratic form concerning the foundations of trades). Manual labor. Why has there never been a worker or peasant mystic who wrote about the use of the disgust of work? This disgust, which is so often there, always threatening -- the soul flees from it and seeks to hide it from itself by a vegetative reaction. There is a danger of death in admitting it to oneself. Such is the source of the lie peculiar to working-class milieus. (There is a lie peculiar to every level.) This disgust is the burden of time. To admit it to oneself without yielding to it is to ascend. Disgust in all its forms is one of the most precious miseries given to man as a ladder for ascending. I have a very large share in this favor. To turn all disgust into disgust with oneself... Monotony is what is most beautiful or most dreadful. Most beautiful if it is a reflection of eternity. Most dreadful if it is the sign of a perpetuity without change. Time transcended or time sterilized. The circle is the symbol of beautiful monotony; pendulum oscillation, of dreadful monotony. Spirituality of work. Work makes one experience in an exhausting way the phenomenon of finality bounced back like a ball: working in order to eat, eating in order to work... If one regards one or the other as an end, or both taken separately, one is lost. The cycle contains the truth. A squirrel turning in its cage, and the rotation of the celestial sphere. Extreme wretchedness and extreme greatness. It is when man sees himself as a squirrel turning in a circular cage that, if he does not lie to himself, he is close to salvation.

The great pain of manual labor is that one is compelled to exert effort for such long hours simply in order to exist. The slave is he for whom no good is proposed as the aim of his toils, except mere existence. He must then either be detached or fall to the vegetative level. No earthly finality separates workers from God. They alone are in this situation. All other conditions imply particular ends that form a screen between man and the pure good. For them, no such screen exists. They do not have something extra of which they must strip themselves. To make effort out of necessity and not for a good -- pushed, not drawn -- in order to maintain one's existence as it is -- that is always servitude. In this sense, the servitude of manual workers is irreducible. Effort without finality. This is terrible -- or more beautiful than anything -- if it is finality without end. The beautiful alone allows one to be satisfied with what is. Workers need poetry more than bread. They need their life to be a poetry. They need a light of eternity. Only religion can be the source of this poetry. It is not religion, it is revolution that is the opium of the people.

The deprivation of this poetry explains every form of demoralization.

Slavery is work without the light of eternity, without poetry, without religion.

Let the eternal light give, not a reason for living and working, but a fullness that dispenses with the search for such a reason.

Failing that, the only incentives are constraint and gain. Constraint, which implies the oppression of the people. Gain, which implies the corruption of the people.

Manual labor. Time entering the body. Through work, man makes himself matter, as Christ does through the Eucharist. Work is like a death.

One must pass through death. One must be killed, must undergo the gravity of the world. The universe weighing on the back of a human being -- what wonder that it hurts?

Work is like a death if it is without incentive. To act while renouncing the fruits of action.

To work -- if one is exhausted, it is to become subject to time like matter. Thought is compelled to pass from one instant to the next without clinging to the past or the future. That is obedience.

Joys parallel to fatigue. Sensory joys. Eating, resting, the pleasures of Sunday... But not money.

No poetry concerning the people is authentic if fatigue is not present in it, and the hunger and thirst born of fatigue.
